items.title: Ecuadorian youth unite against neoliberal models and state violence

s: In Quito, in defiance of the Jóvenes en Acción (Youth in Action) strategy with which Daniel Noboa’s government has attempted to boost employment for young people, thousands of students have been staging marches and sit-ins in streets and squares, demanding medicines, security, and a budget for education.
Their protests show a clear departure from the traditional approach to collective mobilization in Ecuador.

Previously, these types of events have been led by the Confederation of Indigenous Nationalities of Ecuador (CONAIE); trade union groups such as the Ecuador Confederation of Free Trade Union Organizations (CEOSL), the United Workers’ Front (FUT), and the National Union of Educators (UNE); as well as feminist, anti-mining, and environmentalist movements.

However, on the afternoon of Saturday, October 10, 2026, the Ecuadorian capital witnessed a massive mobilization led by high school and university students, who gathered outside the Central University to march to Quito’s Historic Center.
The call was made by the Autonomous Resistance Front (FARO), which comprises several youth collectives:
Quienes encabezaban la marcha anunciaron su finalización y llamaron a dispersarse.
Sin embargo, la multitud continúa avanzando por las calles de Quito, desafiando el asedio policial y haciendo resonar consignas contra el Gobierno de Daniel Noboa. @teleSURtv
What is happening in Quito is striking: Those leading the march announced its conclusion and called for the crowd to disperse.
Nevertheless, the throng continues to move through the streets of Quito, defying a police blockade and chanting slogans against the government of Daniel Noboa.

With their presence in the streets, the young people of Quito denounced the deterioration of public services, including the lack of medical supplies and medicines in hospitals, cuts to the public education budget, low youth employment, a persistent increase in insecurity, and forced disappearances at the hands of state agents.
Their slogans also spoke out against the genocide in Palestine and the United States’ interventionism in Latin America.
According to figures from the National Institute of Statistics and Census (INEC), 40 percent of unemployed people in Ecuador are between 15 and 24 years old.
Labor precariousness, a dearth of opportunities, and the high cost of living are just some of the factors affecting the country’s youth.

Meanwhile, on October 30, the Noboa administration launched its third edition of “Youth in Action,” an initiative aimed at the 18-29 demographic, who are promised temporary, two-month jobs with a salary of USD 400 per month.

The measure has faced harsh criticism from various academics and civic sector representatives, who maintain that the absence of a comprehensive, long-term vision proves its inefficiency in tackling youth unemployment.

In November 2025, Ecuador’s National Assembly approved the country’s 2026 budget proposal, which hit public universities, polytechnic schools, co-financed institutions, and postgraduate programs with an allocated budget reduction of approximately USD 99 million.

The decrease was reflected in the absence of student scholarships, non-existent investment in research, and a reduction in available slots to access free public higher education, which is established as a fundamental right in Article 26 of Ecuador’s Constitution.

During the peaceful youth march, participants chanted slogans like “Out Noboa, out,” “If the people have no peace, the government won’t either,” and “Noboa, fascist,” expressing indignation against a government they believe has failed to solve social problems that affect not only young people, but the majority of the population.
Direct rejection of deficient public administration, coupled with excessive state violence against citizens, motivated the students to protest.
Many videos posted on social media captured police aggression against peaceful demonstrators, as well as physical assaults on journalists as they reported on the protests.
teleSUR reporter Elena Rodríguez Yánez shared her experience on X:

items.title: Trinbagonian Jason Jones wins landmark Privy Council judgement deeming ‘buggery laws’ unconstitutional

s: Trinbagonian LGBTQ+ activist Jason Jones at the Hall of Justice in Port of Spain, Trinidad, after the landmark 2018 judgement that deemed Trinidad and Tobago’s ‘buggery laws’ unconstitutional.
Photo by Maria Nunes, used with permission.

Eight years and nearly seven months after Justice Devindra Rampersad ruled, in the case of LGBTQ+ activist Jason Jones vs. the Attorney General of Trinidad and Tobago, that Sections 13 and 16 of Trinidad and Tobago’s Sexual Offences Act Chapter 11:28 — which criminalise anal sex between consenting adults — were “unconstitutional,” the United Kingdom’s Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, still Trinidad and Tobago’s highest appellate court, overturned a 2025 Court of Appeal decision to keep the country’s “buggery law” on the books.
It has been a long road to get to this point.

Almost as soon as the 2018 judgement went in Jones’ favour, the Trinidad and Tobago government announced its intention to appeal, with then Attorney General Faris Al-Rawi stating, “The rights of equality in the Constitution are clearly expressed.
A first-instance decision is not the only decision to rely upon to settle the law. [An appeal] is only prudent so we can conclusively put the matter to rest.”
Almost seven years later, on March 25, 2025, a local appeal court overturned the 2018 judgement.
Jones was disappointed but not deterred, vowing to take the case all the way to the Privy Council.
He remained true to his word and on November 10, 2026 — quite ironically, given that it was a colonial-era law — British lawlords finally ruled on the matter.

There were a few key issues to be considered, including how to address the controversial “savings law” clause in the legislation — laws enacted prior to colonised countries becoming independent and developing their own constitutions, that were “saved” to remain in force even afterwards.

Jones maintained that the clause had “no place in a 21st century democracy” and that Trinidad and Tobago’s government and parliament were “derelict” in not removing it, especially after the twin-island nation became a republic in 1976.

The Council’s conclusion in the case, which deemed that “Sections 13 and 16 of the SOA 1986 have been shown by Mr Jones ‘not to be reasonably justifiable in a society that has a proper respect for the rights and freedoms of the individual,’” caused it to agree with the 2018 ruling and deny the attorney-general’s cross-appeal.
With other regional territories also using the Privy Council as their highest court of appeal, the result could augur well for similar actions across the wider Caribbean.

As Jones told reporters on the steps of Trinidad’s Hall of Justice following his 2018 triumph, “The human rights issue is not just local […] Over 75 million Commonwealth citizens are criminalised using similar laws — 37 Commonwealth nations — criminalised similarly to Trinidad.”

Still, Jones — who launched his legal challenge in 2015 — says that the fight continues: “Whilst I welcome this judgement, it does not, however, address the main issues of human rights and equality for LGBTQ+ people which have been denied using British colonial-era laws across the Commonwealth and beyond.
It is a stance echoed by many LGBTQ+ organisations, as issues of discrimination, language, and societal and religious acceptance also persist.
Jones is well aware that changing these attitudes requires broader reform and re-education.
The law lords’ unanimous, provisional view, however, was that the original High Court remedy should stand.
However, there may well be written submissions still to come.

items.title: Can regenerative school gardens strengthen food security in Cameroon?

s: The school gardens are helping alleviate food insecurity while providing learning opportunities and empower community members
Students of Blessed Bilingual Education Centre preparing the farm.
Photo by Support Humanity Cameroon.
Used with permission.
Students of Blessed Bilingual Education Centre in Ebang, Cameroon’s Centre Region, have recorded their first harvest of the 2026–2027 school year.

Through the Climate Change and Innovation Club, an initiative introduced in 2024 by Support Humanity Cameroon (SUHUCAM) to connect environmental education with practical action, students planted huckleberry in their school garden at the start of the academic year in September.

Like them, pupils in Cameroon’s North West Region are managing school gardens and growing food using regenerative practices such as minimal tillage, composting, organic manure and fruit-tree grafting.
Cameroon continues to face a decade-long humanitarian crisis, contributing to food insecurity in the Anglophone regions and Far North, while displacing thousands of families.
Earlier this year, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies reported worsening hunger among nearly 6,000 Cameroonian households following an assessment.
More than 3.3 million people were struggling to find enough food, while about 64 percent of households experienced severe food insecurity.
Children are among those affected.
Nationwide, 29 percent of children under five experience chronic malnutrition.
Beyond its nutritional consequences, food insecurity can also affect children’s ability to learn and participate in school activities.
According to the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO), hunger can impair concentration and memory and affect classroom attendance.
In February 2026, the organisation reported that only 2.8 percent of primary school pupils in Cameroon received a free hot meal at school, highlighting the limited reach of school lunch programmes.
Conflict, climate-related disasters, agricultural losses and rising staple food prices are among the main drivers of this crisis.
To combat persistent food insecurity, educators and nonprofit organisations are partnering to teach children how to grow their own food.
In Bamenda, North West region of Cameroon, the Youth Association for Climate Action (YACA) runs the ADAPT Programme, which engages 70 pupils from two nursery and primary schools.

Created after a survey revealed that few schools had gardens or provided environmental education, the ADAPT Club has established gardens with five sections: nurseries, vegetables, fruit trees, composting and tubers.
Muluh Kelly Vughose, Programme coordinator for ADAPT, says pupils are involved in more than just planting.
“Our volunteers, together with the teachers and pupils, designed each garden.
Children are also involved in learning basic agricultural skills like plantain propagation and grafting of fruit trees.
The club holds two sessions each week, lasting about two hours.

In the same region, in Nkambe and neighbouring villages, pupils from six primary and two secondary schools are learning agricultural skills through the Smart School Gardens Project, launched by Youth Development Organisation – Yodo Cameroon.
Schools have received wheelbarrows, watering cans and compost manure to support the project.
“During the two years of implementation, I have watched these pupils and students care for plants from seed germination until harvest,” says Ekoaba Cevie, Yodo Cameroon’s Programme Coordinator.
The gardens produce cabbage, huckleberry, carrots and Irish potatoes.

Meanwhile, SUHUCAM’s regenerative school garden programme in the Centre region combines fruit trees, including guava, soursop, orange and papaya, with plantains and produce such as huckleberry, cabbage and waterleaf.
Through these activities, pupils are learning techniques such as composting, plant propagation and grafting.
Children are embracing the school gardens with enthusiasm, discovering the importance of food production and sustainability through practical experience.
Queeninver Ngwangung, SUHUCAM’s Youth and Advocacy Lead, explains:
“Rather than simply teaching students about sustainable agriculture, food security or climate action, we give them opportunities to practice these concepts,” she said.

“Through growing food, managing organic waste and caring for their gardens, we have observed that students have learnt that environmental solutions can begin with everyday actions within their own schools.”

items.title: Justice is the infrastructure the world keeps forgetting

s: The world cannot build prosperous economies, peaceful societies or resilient democracies while neglecting its people’s everyday justice needs.
This post by Jude Udo Ilo is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “ Justice as infrastructure.
In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law ( HiiL ) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society.
You can support this coverage by donating here.
Imagine visiting a hospital with a serious illness, only to discover that every patient receives the same medication, regardless of their symptoms.
We would rightly call this a failure of healthcare.
Yet this is remarkably close to how justice is delivered in much of the world.
We have built justice systems around institutions rather than people, procedures rather than problems, and legal traditions rather than lived realities.

We measure progress by the number of courts constructed, judges appointed and laws enacted, while paying insufficient attention to whether ordinary people can actually resolve the disputes disrupting their lives.
This institutional obsession reflects a deeper failure in how we understand development.
Justice is not simply a legal service or a moral aspiration.
It is essential for economic and social infrastructure.
Our collective failure to treat it as such is undermining development, deepening inequality and threatening global stability.

With the level of discontent across the world, distrust in institutions, poverty and inequality, and growing footprints of violent conflict, we need to refocus on what is necessary to heal our bleeding world.
When governments and international financial institutions discuss infrastructure, the conversation invariably turns to roads, bridges, electricity and digital connectivity.
These investments matter.
But what happens when a highway project becomes trapped in unresolved land disputes; when a small business cannot recover payments from a supplier?
When a woman cannot claim her inheritance, or communities cannot secure remedies for environmental destruction?
Physical infrastructure cannot deliver its promised benefits when the institutions and mechanisms for resolving grievances are inaccessible, ineffective or distrusted.
Justice is the soft infrastructure that allows economies and societies to function.
For businesses, it provides the certainty necessary for investment, contract enforcement and growth.
For individuals, it protects rights, livelihoods and opportunities.
For communities, it creates peaceful pathways for addressing grievances before they escalate into confrontation.
Without functioning justice systems, economic development becomes fragile and social stability increasingly precarious.

The World Justice Project estimates that the economic costs of legal problems, including lost income, health impacts and expenses of seeking resolution, average 1.7 percent of GDP across the countries studied.
The scale of the problem is staggering.
The Justice for All report estimates that 5.2 billion people lack meaningful access to justice.
HiiL's research demonstrates that everyday legal problems are widespread, while effective, satisfactory resolutions remain elusive.
This is a crisis of development.
Across the world, unresolved grievances are quietly eroding the foundations of social cohesion.
In parts of Africa, disputes over land ownership, natural resources and community rights have contributed to recurring tensions.
In fragile and conflict-affected societies, the absence of credible mechanisms for resolving grievances can deepen mistrust and reinforce cycles of violence.
But justice failures are hardly confined to developing countries.
From housing disputes and discriminatory employment practices to unequal access to legal representation, even wealthy democracies struggle to ensure that justice works for everyone.
The consequences extend beyond those directly affected.
When people repeatedly encounter institutions that cannot protect their rights or resolve their problems, confidence in public authority deteriorates.
When people encounter injustice, they can easily become the enemy of the state.
And where legitimate institutions fail, alternative systems of enforcement emerge.
Sometimes these are constructive community mechanisms.
At other times, they involve coercion, exploitation or violence.
We cannot sustainably address insecurity while ignoring the injustices that help fuel it.

items.title: Restoring social media access comes at a cost in Gabon

s: Citizens in Gabon went 248 days without access to Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, or YouTube
After more than eight months of government blockage, Gabon has restored its social media access.
But it has come at a cost.

This reinstatement comes with a tighter regulatory framework and an unprecedented cooperation between the government and various tech giants, raising serious concerns about freedom of expression and privacy.

On February 17, 2026, Gabon’s media regulator, the High Communication Authority (HAC), suspended major social media networks, including Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube, “until further notice.

According to the regulator, quoted in the daily newspaper L’Essentiel, this measure targeted not only content “undermining national security” but also content involving defamation, cyberbullying, hate speech, and threats to social cohesion.
At first, the suspension had no real impact, with presidential spokesperson Jennyfer Mélodie Sambat claiming it would solely target Meta platforms.

However, according to Gabon Media Time, several influencers, content creators, and citizens later experienced access disruptions on YouTube and TikTok, sometimes rendering connections impossible without a bypass tool, such as a virtual private network (VPN).
The global data platform Internet Society Pulse confirmed this observation, revealing major anomalies for Meta, Telegram, TikTok, and YouTube, but not X (formerly Twitter).
The online news portal Le360 Afrique consequently reported a surge in VPN usage in the months that followed.
For 248 days, more than 1.84 million individuals, or 71.9 percent of the country’s population of over 2.5 million, were denied regular access to some of the world’s most popular digital platforms.
On October 24, 2026, the HAC lifted this suspension, with Africanews stressing that this ruling didn’t necessarily mean a return to business as usual.

It, therefore, remains to be seen whether Gabon, where Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema has been president since September 2023, will restore digital freedoms or establish a new state-controlled online model instead.
A new legal framework, enacted on February 26, 2026, underpins this reinstatement.
According to Gabon Media Time, Ordinance No. 0011/PR/2026 establishes a regulatory framework for digital platform usage, while Ordinance No. 0013/PR/2026 amends the HAC Reorganization Act.

The HAC also invokes a law, enacted on October 5, that ratifies the social media ordinance and establishes a regulatory framework for AI-generated and AI-amplified content, according to reporting by Gabon Review.

What’s more, available data shows that these regulations have introduced joint liability for those who create and share illegal content and require all social media users to provide personal identification information.
Purported as tools to combat abuse, these regulations have raised serious concerns about anonymity, personal data protection, and their stifling effect on public debate.
In a country where criticizing public institutions is politically sensitive, the threat of prosecution for posting online could discourage users from expressing dissent.
The issue here isn’t whether the state should combat cyberbullying, disinformation, or hate speech, but rather how.
While these are valid concerns, the real worry is whether its measures are transparent, proportionate, and subject to independent scrutiny.
The most decisive development in this saga was undoubtedly the unprecedented cooperation between the government and Big Tech companies.
On July 13, 2026, after a meeting at the AI for Good/ WSIS summit in Geneva, Gabonese Minister of Digital Economy Mark-Alexandre Doumba announced an agreement with TikTok.
Both parties signed a 12-month cooperation agreement, ensuring the platform’s compliance with Gabon’s new regulatory framework.
At the meeting, TikTok presented its Q1 2026 content moderation results, revealing that it had removed more than 23,500 pieces of sensitive content in Gabon.
Meanwhile, the HAC confirmed that it had established an “active cooperation” with TikTok, Meta, and YouTube to “improve content moderation.
The regulator added that, during the suspension, it also held direct discussions with these companies.
However, neither the technical details of these exchanges nor the practical operation of the authorities’ reporting tools has been specified.

items.title: In Ukraine, youth are finding their voices in the digital democracy

s: Participants of the Voices of Democracy project in Kyiv, Ukraine.
Photo by beYOUnd.
Used with permission.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South.
It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

The war in Ukraine has created a myriad of challenges for youth and their participation in public life and democratic processes, bringing displacement and misinformation as well as decreased opportunities for political engagement, economic activity, and access to information.
At the same time, there are still avenues youth can pursue to contribute to political decisions and shape the fate of their communities.
Despite the war, people can still submit petitions, participate in public consultations, or advocate for their needs online, but there is a lack of awareness about such opportunities.
Furthermore, vulnerable groups — including displaced persons, minorities, and rural communities — know they have a voice, but struggle to find it.

In 2026, the local non-governmental organization beYOUnd implemented a project to help youth from vulnerable groups acquire the necessary knowledge and skills to find their voices in this new era of digital democracy.
Global Voices conducted an email interview with Yevheniia Holovenko, the chairwoman of beYOUnd, to learn more about their initiative.
The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.
Yevheniia Holovenko (YH): beYOUnd is a youth-led NGO based in Ukraine, registered in October 2025, though we’ve worked as a team long before that.

Our mission is to increase the involvement of vulnerable youth, especially internally displaced people and young people facing difficult social and economic circumstances, in integration, self-realization, and civic life.
Our name reflects our philosophy: it starts with you; it goes beyond!
Our team is largely made up of young people who’ve lived through the same challenges as the youth we work with, which shapes how we approach everything we do.
We joined the Digital Sparks initiative because digital democracy and civic space are exactly where Ukrainian youth need support right now.
Safe, informed participation online is inseparable from resilience during war, and it matched our mission perfectly.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

YH: The war has pushed many young Ukrainians, especially internally displaced persons (IDPs), into digital spaces to stay connected, informed, and civically active, often without the tools to do so safely.
We saw a gap: young people were consuming information and even participating online, but without media literacy, digital security awareness, or confidence that their voice could shape anything.
We wanted to close this gap by developing practical digital safety and civic participation skills in displaced and marginalized youth.
We wanted to give them an opportunity to share ideas on how to increase awareness of digital democracy with the involvement of young people in Ukraine.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?
YH: Within the project “Voices of Democracy in the Digital Era,” we ran an awareness campaign covering digital security, e-participation, and disinformation, which reached over 8,500 views.
On the education side, we delivered three webinars and three workshops on digital democracy, media literacy, civic action planning, and cybersecurity, engaging over a hundred participants.

We also organized an offline networking event in the capital, Kyiv, bringing 27 participants together in person to connect around these same topics, and build on the online learning with real, face-to-face relationships and exchange.

items.title: Ex-lawmaker sentenced to 12.5 years in prison in closed-door trial in Macau

s: Au Kam San's international legal representative called the trial a ‘sham’ with ‘manufactured allegations’
The Chinese territory of Macau recorded its first conviction under the city’s national security law on November 6, 2026, sentencing 69-year-old former lawmaker Au Kam San to 12.5 years in prison.

The Macau Court of First Instance tried the case behind closed doors, and international observers and rights groups have criticized the verdict, calling it a “ bogus prosecution ” that included “serious violations of his right to a fair trial.
The case raises broader questions about how justice is carried out in Macau, and whether its courts offer a fair, open way to challenge the state.
Au served in Macau’s legislature for over 20 years and remained an outspoken current affairs commentator after his retirement in 2021.
He was convicted on one count of subverting state power, three counts of contacting foreign organizations to endanger national security, and one count of violating confidentiality.
According to the court’s statement, the closed-door trial was held on September 16 and 18.
Au was prosecuted under Macau’s domestic security law, enacted on March 3, 2009, and tightened in 2023.

He was accused of cooperating with hostile foreign organizations to collect and disseminate “numerous political propositions that were clearly permeated with [the intent of] subversion of state power” and to assist in the collection and dissemination of false information that intended to incite hatred against the central government, overthrow and undermine the fundamental national system established by the Chinese Constitution, cause foreign countries to take hostile actions against China and Macau, and disrupt the Macau Chief Executive election in 2024.
Au’s family members, several media outlets, and dozens of citizens attended the court’s public sentencing.

Au’s wife, Cheng Miu-shan, responded to the sentencing with an open letter, stating that the closed-door hearing and public sentencing were politically motivated and a baseless persecution to humiliate and smear her husband’s character.
Au’s daughter, Cherry Au, defended her father’s innocence in her interview with UK-based media outlet, the Independent:
“What saddens me the most is seeing him being portrayed as a villain by the very government that he served for so many years,” she said.
“I hope people remember the person they knew throughout his career, the reason why they placed their trust in him and elected him time and again.
Right now he is facing profound injustice.
I hope those who remember his years of service will stand by him.”
Au Kam San has been detained since his arrest in July 2025.

He was initially charged with three counts of “subverting state power,” three counts of “establishing contacts with organizations, groups or individuals outside the Macau Special Administrative Region to commit acts that endanger national security,” and one count of “violating confidentiality.
The court reduced the subversion charge to one count after the closed-door hearing.

After the public sentencing, the court issued a press release stressing that it appointed a lawyer to defend Au and that during the trial, Au did not dispute most of the facts and acknowledged that his collusion with and conspiracy with multiple overseas organizations constituted a crime.
It also pointed out that Au did not stop colluding with foreign and overseas organizations to subvert state power after the 2023 amendment of Macau national security law.
The amendment has expanded the definition of subversive acts from “violent means” to “any illegal means,” to more closely align with Hong Kong’s 2020 version of national security law.
However, Au’s daughter told the press that her father had been barred from contacting his family and accessing a private lawyer to represent him in court.

items.title: From a quiet life to the terror of armed gangs: The story of Haiti’s Kenscoff district

s: On October 19, a unit of Salvadoran soldiers was also ambushed; the situation remains tense
View of the hills from the road from Port-au-Prince to Kenscoff.
Photo by Ketounette via Wikimedia Commons ( CC BY-SA 3.0 ).
In the heights of Pétion-Ville, more than 1,500 metres above sea level, sits the municipality of Kenscoff.
A rural area just 20 kilometres (12.4 miles) southeast of downtown Port-au-Prince, Kenscoff is an idyllic contradiction of sorts.

Its breathtaking landscape is dominated by pine trees and mountain ridges, dotted with terraced gardens and agricultural fields that supply fruit, vegetables and flowers to Port-au-Prince markets, grocery chains and restaurants.
Yet, because of its high elevation, it can also get very cold and foggy, with the sun often setting by five in the afternoon.

The majority of Kenscoff’s residents are peasant farmers, though some wealthy Haitians, craving more peace, quiet, and fresh air, have chosen to leave the nearby urban areas of Port-au-Prince and Pétion-Ville for the area’s pastoral charm and community spirit.
Kenscoff was famous for hosting recreational events where people would come to spend the day, eat fritay (fried foods), ride horses, and visit Fort Jacques, the area’s main historic site.

Visitors would also frequent Ranch le Montcel — now temporarily closed ( burned during gang violence in 2025) — and Chalet Le Refuge, a once popular recreational, social and dining centre, now also closed.

But that was a different Kenscoff, before armed gangs attacked the town in two deadly attacks this year — July 7–8 and August 23–24 — burning down houses, killing 164 people, and kidnapping and displacing others.
Like many other regions in the country, the Kenscoff community suddenly turned from peaceful daily living into being held to ransom by criminal elements.

It all began about two years ago, when the area began to be disrupted by gangs’ attempts to invade the mountains and establish bases there, foiled by the vigilance of residents’ self-defence brigades, with the help of the Haitian police and army.
Yet, every time these attacks occurred, several civilians would be killed, while others abandoned their homes, seeking refuge in the centre of Pétion-Ville, which was less exposed to gang violence.

According to a report by the National Human Rights Defense Network (RNDDH) on the two massacres, the apathy shown by the government and high-ranking security officials, despite warnings, contributed to the scale of the losses.

On September 18, close to a month after the second attack, lawyer, human rights activist and RNDDH Programme Director Rosy Auguste Ducéna detailed what happened during her appearance on the show Se Sa NOU VLE, hosted by Rudy Thomas Sanon on the Team Rudy Officiel YouTube channel.

For its investigation, she said, the RNDDH collected testimonies from various local authorities, including the interim mayor and his deputy chief of staff, the justice of the peace (District judge) and his deputy, the police chief, police officers, members of self-defence brigades, and about 100 victims and their relatives who managed to survive.
But these two massacres were not Kenscoff’s first experience with this type of violence.
The town suffered its first attack from January 27 to 29, 2025, forcing many people to flee to the Kenscoff town hall to find shelter.
There they stayed until Easter 2026, when the interim mayor relocated them to the Afè Nèg Konbit school in the Robin area, which was considered relatively safe.
As the terror of July 7-8 later proved, Ducéna said, this turned out to be a false sense of security:

items.title: The dreamer who wants the world to read Nepali literature

s: ‘We no longer see Nepali literature as something confined by geographical boundaries.’
Rishi Ram Adhikari delivering a speech at the Kitab Jatra Festival held in London in August 2026.
Photo by Kushal Shrestha.
Used with permission.
The Kitab Jatra Festival has quickly become one of the most vibrant platforms for celebrating Nepali literature, books and culture.
The Festival is organised and hosted by the Kitab Yatra Foundation, a Nepal-based organisation promoting literature, reading, art and cultural exchange.

Since its launch in 2018, the festival has grown from a local gathering into a dynamic international event, connecting readers and writers not only across Nepal but also in India, the UK, and the USA, with plans to expand to Dubai, Australia, Portugal, Belgium and Germany.
Working in collaboration with various organisations and institutions, it has created a global stage where Nepali voices are shared, celebrated and amplified.
At the heart of this movement is Rishi Ram Adhikari, Founder and Chairman of the Kitab Yatra Foundation and the Kitab Yatra book distribution company.
In his early 30s, he emerged as a cultural entrepreneur dedicated to promoting Nepali literature and fostering a reading culture.
His initiatives have not only expanded literary festivals abroad but also established over 20 libraries across Nepal and introduced scholarship programs for students.

Recognising these remarkable contributions, Kitab Yatra and Rishi Ram were honoured with the 5th edition of the Tally MSME Honours 2025 and the Public Choice ICT Award in 2019 for their pioneering efforts in enriching the Nepali literary world.
This accolade further highlights his role as one of the leading advocates for Nepali literature today.
Sangita Swechcha from Global Voices interviewed Adhikari via email.
Sangita Swechcha (SS): What inspired you to start the Kitab Yatra book distribution company and the Kitab Jatra Festival at such a young age?
Rishi Ram Adhikari (RRA): My inspiration came from a simple but important realisation: books can transform individuals, and individuals can transform society.
However, for that transformation to happen, books must be accessible, reading must become a habit and literature must be connected to people’s everyday lives.
Through Kitab Yatra, we began working to make books more accessible to readers across Nepal.
But I gradually realised that distributing books alone was not enough.
We also needed to create excitement around reading, bring writers and readers together, and make literature a part of public conversation.
That realisation led to the Kitab Jatra Festival.
In my childhood, I listened to the chanting of my father reciting some slogans [from the epics] Mahabharat and Ramayan.

While studying as a Chartered Accountant (CA) in New Delhi, India, despite my accounting career, I realised the value of words rather than numbers, so I dropped CA and came back to Nepal with four sacks of books and started an online bookstore in Kathmandu, Nepal.
I believe young people should not wait for opportunities to create meaningful change; they should take the initiative to build them.
Our journey has been driven by that belief, along with the dedication of our team, authors, partners and readers.
Book Exhibition at the 7th Edition of Kitab Jatra Festival in Nepal, December 2025.
Photo by Kitab Jatra.
Used with permission.
SS: How has the festival evolved since its beginnings in Nepal in 2018 to now being hosted in countries like the UK, USA, India, Portugal, Belgium, and Germany?
RRA: Since its beginning in 2018, Kitab Jatra has grown from a relatively small literary gathering into a broader platform for literature, culture and meaningful dialogue.

What began with a limited number of voices and a single stage has developed into a festival bringing together writers, artists, thinkers, policymakers, entrepreneurs and readers from different generations.

items.title: Beyond the beaches: The Dominican Republic and the global debate over deep-sea mining

s: The challenge is not solely to declare new protected areas, but ensure they have effective management
The stunning beauty of the Dominican Republic’s north coast at Los Haitises National Park.
Photo by Jason Boldero on Flickr ( CC BY 2.0 ).

When you think of the Dominican Republic, the first thing that might come to mind is paradise where sun, sand, and sea combine to offer unforgettable experiences to Dominican families and global travellers alike — but the country’s deep sea is also of critical importance.

Jonathan Delance, director of conservation of the National 30×30 Program of the Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources, says that Dominican marine ecosystems are one of the country’s “greatest natural and strategic riches” — diverse, highly connected, and fundamental to national life.
From an ecological standpoint, coral reefs, mangroves, seagrass beds, dunes, beaches, pelagic zones, and deep-sea ecosystems sustain biodiversity.
From an economic and social standpoint, they are the foundation of tourism, fishing, and coastal protection.
Despite relevant research being conducted in the country, information remains limited.
According to Delance, some of the available studies on Dominican deep waters have had a geophysical, geochemical, or geological focus, rather than an ecological one.

This is largely because deep-sea research is expensive, complex, and requires specialised technology, such as remotely operated vehicles, acoustic equipment, deep-sea cameras, and highly specific taxonomic capabilities.

Precisely because of these limitations, for a long time the National System of Protected Areas lacked a clear representation of deep ecosystems and their underwater geomorphologies, a gap that began to close with the inclusion of the Beata Underwater Ridge as a conservation object within the Orlando Jorge Mera Marine Sanctuary, representing a relevant step forward for the country.

As part of the scientific basis for this process, Delance explains that the technical report on deep-sea fauna documented research between 900 and 4,200 metres deep, recording 1,855 biological observations and 3,294 organisms.

One of the most interesting finds was 148 morphospecies, defined in the book Marine Biodiversity as a “group of specimens that can be distinguished from others on the basis of morphological characteristics,” including poriferans, cnidarians, echinoderms, chordates, arthropods, annelids, mollusks, and other yet undetermined organisms.
The pelagic fauna expedition conducted in 2024 covered 2,771 kilometres (1,722 miles) and identified six species of cetaceans, 15 species of birds, as well as sharks and turtle routes.
Environmental DNA resulted in the identification of species — including more than 400 morphospecies — along the entire food chain, demonstrating the health and complexity of this space.

Despite these advances, Delance notes, important gaps persist: “We need more information on taxonomic identification at the species level, genetic connectivity, oceanographic dynamics, seasonal distribution, cumulative impacts, biogeography of deep species, and the response of these ecosystems to underwater disturbances, climate change, and other pressures.”

According to the International Seabed Authority (ISA), deep-sea mining (DSM) refers to the extraction of mineral resources from deposits located on the deep seabed, typically found between 400 metres (1.300 feet) and 6.5 kilometres (4 miles) beneath the ocean’s surface.
There are three primary types of mineral deposits.

Polymetallic nodules (PMN) were discovered on March 7, 1873, during the Challenger expedition; scientists described them as “several peculiar black oval bodies which were composed of almost pure manganese oxide.
The ISA states that they are composed of manganese, iron, silicates, and hydroxides, and can be as small as micro-nodules or as large as 20 centimetres.
They are commonly found on the west coast of Mexico in the Pacific Ocean (also known as the Clarion-Clipperton Fracture Zone), as well as the Central Indian Ocean Basin, and the Peru Basin.

While polymetallic nodules can be found in lakes, the ones with greater economic value are typically located at depths of 4,000–6,000 metres (2.5 miles–3.7 miles), in areas with an extremely low sedimentation rate.

items.title: How people in Montenegro are making their country cleaner

s: This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South.
It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.
Montenegro is on its way to joining the EU; at the moment, the goal is to do so by 2028.

The United Nations Economic Commission for Europe ( UNECE) review in 2025 states that the country has made significant progress in aligning its environmental legal and regulatory framework, as well as much of its national legislation, with European Union (EU) directives.
However, some problems remain, including waste management and a very low recycling rate — less than 2 percent, far below the EU’s 50 percent target.

Austrian Member of Parliament Thomas Waitz (Greens/EFA), chair of the delegation to the EU-Montenegro Stabilisation and Association Parliamentary Committee, said in an interview with The New Union Post that there have been “massive improvements” in Montenegro, citing as an example the closure of more than 100 illegal landfills in the last year: “It is a great effort for such a small country.
But they have another 500, and if we expected them to have them all cleaned up, it would be impossible.”

While politicians and international agencies discuss how Montenegro could get closer to the target and put its waste management under control, ordinary citizens are making practical steps to improve the situation today.
This Digital Spark spotlight story is about one such organization, EkoGard, and the many people who participate in its efforts and, step by step, try to make Montenegro cleaner.
Global Voices interviewed the organization’s founder and general director, Senad Pepić, about the impact of Digital Spark and its community initiative.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Spark project.
Senad Pepić (SP): EkoGard was built through years of work on the ground, not in an office.
It grew out of the Očistimo Rožaje initiative, where we spent six years building a strong community of people ready to take action.
We started with illegal dumpsites, but our work gradually expanded to other environmental and social issues affecting everyday life.
We organized cleanups, worked with young people, launched campaigns, and encouraged residents to tackle problems that kept coming back.
We joined Digital Spark because we wanted to bring what we learned in the field together with digital tools and data.
We hoped to show a fuller picture of the problems and change how people talk about them.
EkoMapa grew out of that idea as a natural next step in our work.
GV: What issue or challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?
SP: One cleanup in particular made us rethink our approach.
We cleared an illegal dumpsite beside a rural road, in an area where residents had no suitable place to dispose of their waste.
The nearest legal disposal point was about six kilometers away.
After the cleanup, we asked for a waste container to be installed and were promised that the problem would be addressed.
Three years passed; the container was never installed, and the dumpsite returned.
Its return changed how we saw similar sites elsewhere.
We had photos, posts, and letters from other areas, but no way to see the full extent of the problem or how it related to gaps in waste collection services.
We wanted to map these places and understand the conditions in each settlement.
Doing that gives us a way to show local institutions where waste disposal services are lacking and talk about what needs to change.

items.title: Big Tech, AI, and the quiet expansion of digital surveillance in Nigeria

s: How much control do people retain over their personal information in a world increasingly shaped by AI?
Every search, social media interaction, and conversation with an artificial intelligence (AI) tool can leave behind information about its user.
Individually, these digital traces may appear insignificant.
Collectively, however, they can reveal interests, habits, preferences and patterns of behavior that have considerable commercial and political value.
As AI becomes increasingly embedded in everyday life, technology companies are finding new ways to use data to develop their products, personalize services and generate revenue.
While these developments offer considerable benefits, they also raise a difficult question: How much control do people retain over their personal information in a world increasingly shaped by AI?
The issue extends beyond privacy policies and user agreements.

It concerns the growing power of technology companies to collect information, draw conclusions about individuals, and influence the digital environments in which people communicate, work, and access information.

In September 2024, the United States Federal Trade Commission (FTC) published findings from an investigation into nine major social media and video-streaming companies, including Meta, YouTube, TikTok, and Amazon-owned Twitch.
The FTC reported that these companies collected extensive information about users and, in some cases, non-users.
The information included personal details, interests, online activities, and data obtained from other sources.
The investigation also raised concerns about lengthy data retention, inadequate privacy protections, and the use of personal information in automated systems, including AI.

The report highlighted a fundamental imbalance: Companies can accumulate substantial information about individuals, while those individuals may have limited understanding of how their data is used or how to prevent certain uses.
AI adds another dimension to this problem.
Data can help train models, improve recommendations, and power automated decisions.
However, the greater the volume and variety of information companies can access, the more important it becomes to establish clear limits on its collection and use.
The concern is not that every company collecting data is necessarily acting maliciously.
Rather, it is that systems designed to maximize commercial value from information can create incentives to collect more data than people reasonably expect or understand.
For millions of people, AI offers opportunities that were previously difficult to access.
Students can use AI tools to support learning, small businesses can improve their operations, and journalists can explore new approaches to research and production.
In countries such as Nigeria, where access to resources and professional services can be uneven, these tools could help narrow certain gaps.
AI systems that support local languages and reflect diverse cultural experiences could also make digital services more accessible.
Yet inclusion should mean more than allowing people to use a technology.
It should also mean ensuring that they understand the conditions under which they use it and retain meaningful rights over their information.
Many digital services are governed by lengthy terms and privacy policies that users may accept without fully understanding the implications.
Some AI products also raise questions about whether information submitted through prompts, uploaded documents, or other interactions may be retained or used to improve models.
The precise practices differ between companies and products.
Nevertheless, users need clear explanations of what information is collected, why it is needed, how long it is retained, and whether it may be used for purposes beyond the immediate service.
Without these safeguards, the benefits of AI inclusion risk coming with an invisible cost: reduced control over personal information.
The connection between big tech and authoritarianism requires careful examination.
Authoritarianism is not simply the collection of data by private companies.
It involves the concentration and exercise of power in ways that undermine accountability, rights, and freedoms.
However, extensive corporate data collection can create conditions that make surveillance easier.
Detailed personal information can support profiling, targeted persuasion and the prediction of individual behavior.
Depending on the circumstances, businesses, governments, or other actors may exploit these capabilities.

items.title: Global Voices condemns the attacks on Albanian fact-checking service Faktoje

s: Faktoje is a respected member of the international fact-checking community

Since October 27, at least 20 online media outlets and social media accounts in Albania have been waging a coordinated attack against the staff of fact-checking media service Faktoje Center, based in Tirana.
A partner of Global Voices, Faktoje has been promoting accountability based on the right to information and transparency since 2018.

Faktoje and its team members, in particular its director, Klodiana Kapo, are facing a series of coordinated attacks from media outlets that have been circulating and reproducing articles that question Faktoje’s funding, financial management and independence, using its publicly available financial statements to cast doubt on the organisation’s credibility.
Faktoje is a certified signatory of the Code of Principles of the International Fact-Finding Network and the Code of Standards of the European Fact-Checking Standards Network.
Both require high levels of public transparency in disclosing sources of funding and methodologies of work.

This coordinated campaign aims to undermine the impact of Faktoje’s important work by maliciously using financial information that the organization voluntarily publishes, but stripping it of context and mischaracterizing its influence.

Faktoje considers these attacks to be directly connected to its fact-checking activities under its partnership with Meta, in the context of its recent fact-checking work covering the ongoing protests and debunking misleading narratives targeting protesters.

Since its inception eight years ago, Faktoje has stood at the forefront of the fight for freedom of expression, independent journalism, and information integrity in Albania and the wider Balkans region, including participation in the regional Western Balkans Anti-Disinformation Hub, the Anti-Disinformation Network for the Balkans and the continent-wide European Digital Media Observatory – EDMO Network.
Faktoje is a respected member of the international fact-checking community.

Albanian authorities and European institutions need to speak up publicly for independent fact-checkers and journalists, and to ensure their safety, while media outlets reporting on civil society funding need to do so accurately and in context.
Global Voices joins the European Fact-Checking Standards Network and the International Fact-Checking Network in vehemently condemning those attacks on our partner.
We stand in solidarity with our colleagues.

items.title: Venezuela welcomes opposition leader María Corina Machado home

s: María Corina Machado arriving in Caracas after months of hiding and exile.
Photo by Óscar Calles, 2026.
Used with permission.

Thousands of people took to the Valle-Coche highway in Caracas to welcome the opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize laureate María Corina Machado, who returned to Venezuela after 16 months in hiding and ten months in exile.
The massive gathering was one of celebration, but her compatriots were also filled with doubts about what comes next.

After more than a year in the shadows, forced into hiding following her kidnapping — allegedly by government paramilitaries — at her last public protest in 2025, Machado quietly slipped out of the country.

She emerged on the global stage later that year to receive the Nobel Peace Prize honoring her social organization campaign during Venezuela’s 2024 presidential elections, which were ultimately stolen by Nicolás Maduro.

Since the former Venezuelan president’s capture on January 3, 2026, Machado has tried — and failed — to enter the country on at least seven occasions, claiming that the administration established by U.S.
President Donald Trump didn’t allow her in.

On the morning of October 25, however, Machado was spotted in the city of Barquisimeto, where she visited the Santa Rosa church, and at about 10:25 that evening, her caravan passed through Santa Mónica, along the main route that leads to Venezuela’s captital:
Drivers excitedly honked their horns; in a crowd of about 3,000, people shouted slogans.
Starting from the state of Lara, Machado’s caravan crossed Yaracuy, Carabobo, and Aragua as it inched toward Caracas — a journey of more than 300 kilometres that took her nearly 11 hours to complete.

On the heels of the January 3 United States military operation that captured Nicolás Maduro, whose 2024 re-election was questioned both inside and outside of Venezuela, then vice president Delcy Rodríguez took over as interim president.
Since August, her interim government has been negotiating with Dinorah Figuera, president of the National Assembly who was elected in 2015, in a Washington-driven dialogue process.
Despite having promoted participation in the 2024 presidential elections, Machado’s party, Vente Venezuela, has had no representation in those negotiations.
The crowd waited for hours for Maria Corina Machado's arrival to the capital city.
Photo by Óscar Calles, 2026.
Used with permission.
Yet, U.S.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio attributed Machado’s safe return to those talks, which he claimed had already allowed for the release of hundreds of political prisoners and the return of hundreds of exiled opposition figures.
Rubio called on all political actors to back them because they represent “the best opportunity Venezuela has had in thirty years.”

Faced with political demobilization, Venezuelans are used to seeing protests where the majority of participants are activists, leaders, and members of civil society organizations — people who are well-informed because it is their job to be — but Machado’s gathering was different.
There were people without party shirts or hats; just a combination of families, friends, and civilians who seemed motivated by her return and hopeful for their country.
People began to assemble on the highway around 3:00 p.m. local time.
After hours of waiting, the gathering turned into a party — the type of celebration that many did not dare to have after January 3.
Machado barely spoke; she did not have a megaphone and was in the tray of a pickup truck with a security detail around her.
She gave no statements to the media during the caravan; instead, she listened to and greeted the crowd, hugging people, touching their hands, and letting herself be seen.
On this occasion, people did not go to hear proposals, but simply to see her.
October’s Spotlight contributors illuminated a range of political, economic, and geographic contexts

Fifteen years ago I wrote an article about “networked authoritarianism,” describing China as “exhibit A” for how an authoritarian state adapts to the internet and then adapts digital technologies to increase its own power.
I sought to counter prevailing narratives of the time that the internet and tech companies were intrinsically a liberating, democratizing force.
While such narratives were eventually discredited, we must not give up on our ability to use technology to defend and exercise our rights.
Nor can we simply demand that governments and companies solve the problems they jointly continue to create.
October’s spotlight on Big Tech and Authoritarianism explored a range of relationships between tech companies and political actors across the global majority.
Power is wielded through digital technologies in many ways.
There are no quick fixes or easy solutions to stop abuses.

But we are not helpless: our Global Voices community has a role to play in strengthening solidarity and cooperation among people fighting to defend their rights, hold abusers accountable, and claim agency over our information environments.
Spotlight contributors illuminated a range of political, economic, and geographic contexts: from Brazil to Hong Kong, Kenya, Myanmar, Palestine, Venezuela, Xinjiang and beyond.

They’ve told stories of how different types of governments (or sometimes political insurgents) leverage geopolitical alliances, relationships with tech companies, regulatory power, or other advantages in order to expand political or military dominance, manipulate public opinion, or exercise direct control over citizens.
Meanwhile, companies use their own technologies, resources, and government relationships to expand market access and profit.
Tech power is often wielded in ways that make it harder for ordinary people to fight back against abuses.
In some cases it is difficult, if not impossible, to prove who has committed what abuse and whether it was intentional — even while harm to individuals or communities has clearly occurred.
In other cases, companies discover abuse of their systems to threaten, silence, surveil, or mislead users only after the damage has been done.
In Brazil, one expert warns of “governance washing.
An NGO leader working in West Asia and North Africa warns of the rise of a cottage industry of organizations focused on tech accountability without measurably preventing harms.
In North America and Europe, government regulation of Big Tech is often touted as a silver bullet for protecting citizens from harm.

But stories from Bangladesh, Kenya and the DRC illustrate different ways that without rigorous safeguards, regulation and enforcement in the name of holding Big Tech accountable can be abused by governments to threaten, track, or discredit critics and political rivals.
Our contributors pointed to conditions that must be met if we are to prevent government abuse of regulations.
Laws and regulations need to be evaluated for their compatibility with human rights standards, and reformed or rejected if they fall short.

Citizens — through the free press, watchdog NGOs, whistleblower protections and grievance mechanisms — need to be able to monitor and document harms and abuses with clear process for redress and remedy.
Sadly, most democracies fail to hold governments — let alone companies — accountable for protecting human rights.
Then there is the even harder problem of what multinational companies should do after a coup or military takeover, leaving users’ data exposed with deadly consequences.
Such cases underscore the vital importance of encryption, data security training for civil society, and corporate data minimization practices.
A number of stories describe how global powers leverage their national tech companies to advance strategic and economic interests well beyond their own borders.
The companies in turn benefit from such relationships to expand their own global market access, serving as opaque information intermediaries and channels of digital infrastructure.

items.title: The scandals and suspects surrounding Flávio Bolsonaro, according to the Brazilian press

s: After being defeated in the elections, the senator fled to the US with his family
Art by Global Voices with Canva Pro.
Photo by the Brazilian Senate. Fair use.

Forty-eight hours after losing the runoff in Brazil to incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Flávio Bolsonaro, former president Jair Bolsonaro ’s eldest son, a senator representing Rio de Janeiro, fled to the United States.

From there, where his brother Eduardo, a former congressman, has lived since February 2025, he continues to challenge the results of the election he lost by 4.4 million votes, as attested by the Electoral Court (TSE), the Organization of American States (OAS), and other right-led governments in the region.
Upon landing in Miami, Flávio published a letter proclaiming himself “the true president of Brazil” and “president-elect of Brazil.
After 22 minutes — and a demand from the US Department of State — he retracted to “the leader of Brazil.”
US President Donald Trump had said that Brazil’s elections “ looked rigged,” but he wouldn't “ get involved.
The New York Times reported, however, that Flávio was helped by Trump's aides.
“The jet [he traveled on] had been arranged by a White House official,” affirmed the newspaper.

Flávio’s narrative is that he is being persecuted by the Brazilian justice system and Lula’s government as an opposition leader, since the Supreme Court ordered the seizure of his passports — he also has Italian citizenship — right after his defeat was announced.

Justice Alexandre de Moraes, considered a foe of the Bolsonaro family and himself under suspicion for having links to the same disgraced banker connected to Flávio, issued the order in response to a Federal Police request that considered Flávio a flight risk.
In Brazil, a president cannot be investigated for alleged crimes committed before their term, meaning that once elected, all pending investigations involving Flávio would have been suspended.
This is also the first time in 24 years that Flávio will not have a seat to ensure his parliamentary immunity.

According to the Brazilian Federal Police, three elements indicated a flight risk in Flávio’s case: an interview his brother Eduardo gave to a podcast in the US defending the idea of him leaving the country, on October 23, his considerable economic power, and well-established structures abroad that could support him in a long stay.

The day after the election, after visiting his father, who is under house arrest convicted for a coup attempt, Flávio recorded a video complaining about the measure, claiming “he never thought about leaving the country” and promising to stay and answer to investigations.
Overnight, apparently, he had a change of heart in time for a new plan.
Investigations and corruption suspicions have long surrounded his name.

In 2020, Sergio Moro, the judge who convicted Lula, resigned as Bolsonaro’s justice minister, accusing the president of trying to intervene with the Federal Police to protect Flávio in an embezzlement and money-laundering inquiry.
In a cabinet meeting, then-president Bolsonaro shouted at his ministers: “I won’t wait until they fuck my entire family,” saying he would fire whoever got in their way.
During this election campaign, skeletons in Flávio's closet were further exposed in stories published by the Brazilian press.
Global Voices gathered the main ones here.
Flávio is currently under three investigations at the Supreme Court.
This is the case that led Jair Bolsonaro to allegedly interfere in the Federal Police in 2020.
Flávio was indicted by Rio’s Public Prosecution Office for embezzlement, money laundering, and criminal organization.
The case was later adjourned.
Rachadinha (“split” in English) is a salary kickback scheme in which a politician hires someone for a certain position and then reclaims part of their salary.

items.title: Unmarried Chinese women are rewriting the marriage script

s: Chinese women are challenging marriage pressures and redefining what it means to be single.
The marriage market at People’s Park in Shanghai, 2013.
Photo by Jpbowen via Wikimedia Commons, licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0.
On weekends at Shanghai’s People’s Park, umbrellas covered with handwritten sheets of paper line the paths.
Parents stand beside them, exchanging information about their unmarried children: age, height, education, income, and whether they own an apartment.
It is one of China’s most famous marriage markets — a place where private hopes and social expectations meet in public since 2005.
For years, the word shengnü (剩女), literally translated as “leftover women,” hovered over many of the women whose profiles appeared there.
The translation sounds strange in English because the original Chinese carries a sharper meaning.
The character sheng (剩) does not simply mean “remaining.
It suggests something left behind, something unused.
In everyday contexts, it can describe leftover food — something that has passed its ideal moment and may eventually be discarded.

When the term became popular in China in the late 2000s, it was used to describe unmarried urban women, often highly educated professionals, who were considered “too old” for marriage after their late twenties.
The label was not just a description of marital status.
It turned a personal choice into a social judgment.
But today, if you search Chinese media, the phrase shengnü appears far less frequently than it once did.

Instead, a more neutral term, zhonggnü (中女), literally translated as “middle or in-and-between women,” is now more often used to describe unmarried women in their thirties in both mainstream media and social platforms.
While the word has faded, many of the expectations behind it remain.
The language around unmarried women has become more circumspect, though still pointed.

Instead of openly calling women “leftover,” conversations often appear in softer forms: concerns about women being “too picky,” warnings about missing the “best age” for marriage and childbirth, or questions about why a successful woman still has not found a partner.

Instead of using the neutral term zhonggnü, which still highlights women’s age, some women have created new terms and spaces on social media platforms, such as Xiaohongshu and Douban, to discuss these pressures on their own terms.
For example, they have reframed the marriage debate to cuīhūn (催婚) — the repeated pressure from family members to marry — and kǒnghūn (恐婚) — the fear or hesitation surrounding marriage itself.
These words reveal a shift.
The conversation is no longer only about why women are failing to meet expectations.
Increasingly, women are asking whether those expectations should be followed at all.
On Xiaohongshu, a user writing under the name “十元尼美” (Ten Yuan Nimei) described seven years of pressure to marry, beginning when she graduated from university.
By 30, she wrote, the pressure had eased — not because her family had accepted her choices, but because people arranging introductions considered her too old for the matchmaking market.
At 34, she said, her parents had almost stopped asking.
Her advice to other women began with creating physical distance.
Moving from her home province of Hunan to Beijing had largely confined her parents’ pressure to phone calls; later, she moved to Spain.
“Sometimes, freedom comes not from persuasion, but from distance,” she wrote.
Other posts question the pressure itself.
One shared by the account “渭北春天树” carried the title —“Pressuring someone to marry is, at its core, a form of expulsion.
(催婚的本质是一种驱逐) These conversations no longer see shengnü or unmarried women as a problem, but are turning the conversation on its head to scrutinize traditional conservative family values.

items.title: Tracing the recruitment trap behind Russia’s war

s: No justice for Bangladeshi workers who are recruited into Russia’s war
War-wounded Bangladeshis in Russia plead to return home.
Screenshot from a YouTube report by Ekhon TV. Fair use.
Maksudur Rahman was 31 when a labor recruiter arrived in his hometown in Lakshmipur district, southeastern Bangladesh, with a job offer: becoming a janitor in Russia.
Nearly every family in the district has someone working overseas, so the pitch landed.
According to an international investigation, he borrowed money and paid the broker BDT 1.2 million (about USD 9,800).
For a household like his, that is a fortune, but the promised wages made the debt look manageable.
He signed up and flew out.
What followed had nothing to do with brooms.
Within weeks, he was on the front lines of Russia’s war in Ukraine.
He and three other Bangladeshi workers were handed a paper written in Russian — a language they did not understand — and told to sign.
Then came an army camp, where recruits were trained in drone tactics, medical evacuation, and heavy weapons.
When Rahman protested, a Russian commander replied through a translation app that his own agent had sent him there.
Workers in his group were threatened with ten-year jail terms and beaten, he said.
His story is a case study in how this insidious war pipeline operates: a local agent, a borrowed fortune, a contract nobody could read, and a war that was never part of the bargain.
But to understand how a man from Lakshmipur ended up in that camp, it’s important to look at the realities in Russia and what is driving these recruitment traps.
Russia has a manpower problem, and the figures are hard to wave away.
Enlistment into contract service dropped about 20 percent in the first quarter of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, according to international reporting relayed by Ukrainian outlets.
This deficit persists even though Moscow is offering signing packages of up to USD 80,000 and debt write-offs of up to USD 140,000.
Meanwhile, BBC and Mediazona journalists estimate there have been at least 300,000 Russian deaths since the war began on February 24, 2022, based on local obituaries.
Other Western intelligence estimates put Russian deaths near 500,000, with monthly casualties of 30,000 to 35,000.
One estimate says the country needs another 1.5 million workers to stabilize its labor market, and officials themselves expect a shortfall of 3.1 million people by 2030.
Because stricter migration rules have also pushed out roughly a million temporary workers, the army and the factories now compete for the same shrinking labor pool.

While Russia has not dared to implement another full-scale military draft as it did in September 2022 — a move that was highly damaging to the regime and local support — officials are doing everything they can to buy recruits or force those who are vulnerable, elderly, or simply went to the draft station to register to go to the front lines.
Given these manpower challenges, Moscow has looked outward.
It has already used tens of thousands of prisoners and three waves of North Korean troops, yet that wasn’t enough.

A UK defense assessment, summarized by a Ukrainian outlet, says the supply of convict recruits is probably exhausted, and Russia is widening its search across the Global South to avoid another mobilization at home.
Ukrainian data counts nearly 29,000 foreigners who have signed contracts since 2022.
One report says the army wants at least 18,500 more in 2026, naming Bangladesh among its top targets.
Rights groups see a pattern behind these numbers.

The International Federation for Human Rights described an organized pipeline aimed at undocumented migrants, detainees, precarious workers, and foreign students across three continents, and Amnesty International accused Moscow last month of deceptive, coercive, and exploitative recruitment.

items.title: Egypt’s crackdown on independent media reaches Mada Masr as editor faces trial

s: Egypt convicted Mada Masr's Lina Attalah in a hearing marred by violations and ordered it closed
Lina Attalah.
Picture from Mada Masr website.
Used with permission.

The latest wave of suppression of the country’s last remaining critical voices began with the violent arrest of the entire newsroom of Matsada2sh, a fact-checking and open-source intelligence (OSINT) page that relies on social media and is run by young journalists.
The six-person team was forcibly disappeared, illegally detained, and interrogated under torture for several days before being charged with terrorism and spreading false news.
They remain in pretrial detention.
The crackdown then reached Mada Masr, one of Egypt’s most prominent independent outlets, and its founder and editor-in-chief, Lina Attalah.
On November 11, Attalah is due to stand trial for the second time in two weeks, this time on charges of spreading false news that carry a possible prison sentence.
The new trial follows her conviction on October 27, when a court found her guilty of managing a news website without a license in a single hearing marred by violations of her right to a fair trial.
She was given the maximum fine of EGP 3 million (about USD 55,000) and was forcibly removed from the courtroom and held until the fine was paid, seven hours later.
The court also ordered Mada Masr shut down and all of its equipment confiscated.
According to Mada Masr, the judge appointed a lawyer to represent Attalah even though eight of her own lawyers were in the courtroom and she objected.
The outlet says her objection was not recorded in the session’s minutes.
Amnesty International reports that Mada Masr applied for a license from the Supreme Council for Media Regulation in 2018 and 2020 and received no response, and submitted a new application in 2026.
Mada Masr was founded in 2013, an independent, critical, investigative outlet.
In other a decade of operation, Mada Masr was instrumental in informing the public about what is happening in Egypt, as well as in the region.
It gave a platform to torture victims and the families of political prisoners, and created space for debate on reproductive rights.
Its reporting on the genocides in Sudan and Gaza uncovered abuses and stood with refugees facing xenophobic attacks and security crackdowns.
The outlet has also long engaged with technology issues and advocated for a free, independent internet for the global majority.
The attack comes at a crucial point in Egypt’s and the region’s history, and goes beyond a question of human rights or activism.
At least 25 journalists are currently imprisoned in Egypt.

On Friday 30 October, Mada Masr published a statement on Instagram describing an “ongoing battle” and its efforts at “finding a legal way to continue [its] work while also taking care of each other in this moment of madness.
A wave of solidarity has mobilized supporters in Egypt and abroad.
“This is the kind of social movement, the doing of politics, how a newsroom is connected to its community, that we in our everyday practice would want to write about.
But this time it is us whom it was happening to,” the statement reads.
It concludes: “We are angry but hopeful, we are tired but insistent that our work must go on, that Lina should face neither prison nor fines, that all jailed journalists should be free.”

A joint statement led by Amnesty International and signed by organizations worldwide condemned “in the strongest terms the conviction of Lina Attalah, and the court’s order to shut down one of the country’s leading and last remaining independent newsrooms.
It called on Egyptian authorities to allow Mada Masr to operate freely.

items.title: In Kosovo, a new app makes reporting problems to the government fast and easy

s: It will cut the bureacratic red tape that plagues state institutions

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South.
It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.
One of the biggest barriers for people’s effective engagement with the authorities in Kosovo is a confusing and unresponsive bureaucracy.

Whenever citizens want to report a problem in their community, such as potholes or illegal waste disposal, they are met with a system that requires them to know the roles and responsibilities of various state institutions and handle necessary paperwork themselves.

When submitted to the wrong agency or without proper documents, citizens’ complaints are either ignored or can take long periods to be processed, which discourages engagement and has an adverse effect on people’s trust in the government.
Ultimately, it deteriorates the already challenging situation regarding transparency, communication, and accountability of state bodies in Kosovo.

In 2026, a local non-governmental organization (NGO), Sbunker, responded to this challenge by creating an online platform called Kosovo.report to help citizens report their complaints to the authorities in a quick and easy manner.
Global Voices conducted an email interview with Hana Deva, project manager at SBunker, to learn more about their initiative.
The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.

Hana Deva (HD): Sbunker is a non-governmental organization founded in 2016, focused on providing analysis and informed perspectives on important political, economic, social, and cultural issues in Kosovo and the Western Balkans.
Through our Disinfo program, we monitor local and regional media content to identify and address disinformation.
Sbunker produces podcasts and other media content exploring political and social developments, philosophical, cultural, and theoretical discussions.
We joined the Digital Sparks project because we wanted to create a direct form of civic engagement through technology.
This led to the development of Kosovo.report, a platform designed to give citizens a simple way to report problems and submit requests concerning their neighborhoods and local communities.
The platform is intended to act as a link between citizens and public institutions by helping these reports reach the relevant institutions and making the process more accessible to the citizens.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?
HD: Through our work in media and civic engagement, we became interested in how citizens communicate everyday problems in their communities to public institutions.
