Research on public administration in Kosovo points to fragmented public service delivery, inconsistencies in administrative procedures and digital services, and continuing challenges in communication between citizens and institutions.
This can make the process of reporting an issue to the right department unclear.
Kosovo.report was developed with this challenge in mind.
The idea is to give citizens a more straightforward way to report an issue, without requiring them to first determine which institution or department is responsible.
Based on the type and location of the problem, the platform is designed to route the report to the appropriate department and allow the citizen to follow what happens afterwards.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?
HD: Our main work has been the development of Kosovo.report, from the initial concept to a functional platform now being prepared for its pilot phase.

Alongside this development, we have coordinated with the Municipality of Prishtina to determine how reports should reach the appropriate departments, and prepared a Memorandum of Understanding to formalise this cooperation.

items.title: Unpacking Hong Kong’s rule of law score according to the World Justice Project’s ranking

s: Hong Kong ranks 24th in rule of law index and is trending down

The Hong Kong anti-graft body, the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC), flaunted on X in early October that the city ranked in the top 10 globally and third in Asia in the “Absence of Corruption” category on the “ Rule of Law Index 2026 ” published by the World Justice Project (WJP).

However, the “Absence of Corruption” merely captures whether or not public officials from the administration, police force, and judiciary use their offices for private gain; this single factor does not mean a society is free from corruption, as institutional favoritism, such as political nepotism, legal discrimination, and cronyism, are equally dangerous abuses of power that create systematic injustice.

That’s why the WJP includes eight major factors in its index, and Hong Kong ranks 24th and scored 0.71 in the overall index among 143 countries, falling behind Australia (12), Singapore (14), Japan (15), and South Korea (20) in Asia and the Pacific.
Between 2016 and 2020, Hong Kong consistently ranked 16th overall in the index.

The eight factors considered in the Rule of Law Index are “constraints on government power,” “absence of corruption,” “open government,” “fundamental rights,” “order and security,” “regulatory enforcement,” “civil justice,” and “criminal justice.”

Hong Kong performs best in “order and security” (ranked seventh with a 0.92 score), “absence of corruption” (ranked 10th with a 0.83 score), and “regulatory enforcement (ranked 16th with a 0.79 score).
Among the subfactors of “order and security,” the city indeed has a relatively low crime rate (ranked eighth), and near-zero violent expression of grievance (ranked ninth).
In fact, the city has had hardly any protests since 2021, following the enactment of the National Security Law on June 30, 2020, and a heavy-handed crackdown on unauthorized protests.
However, civic conflict remains high (ranked 40th), as people resort to street fights to express their frustrations.

The average Hongkonger will likely disagree with the relatively high ranking of “regulatory enforcement,” particularly after the recent release of the Taipo Deadly Fire investigation report, which revealed that multiple Hong Kong government authorities, including the Housing Bureau, the Labor Department, the Fire Service Department, and the Buildings Department, had not effectively enforced related regulations, which could have prevented the death of 168 individuals on November 25, 2025.

Moreover, while Hongkongers have complained about tender rigging in building renovations for over a decade, it was only after the high-profile Taipo fire that the authorities vowed to actively investigate the construction sector.
Some fire victims also criticized the government’s buy-back plan as disrespectful of their private property rights.
Both effectiveness of regulatory enforcement and respecting property rights are subfactors of “regulatory enforcement” in the Index.
Hong Kong’s worst performance among the eight categories is “constraints in government’s power” (ranked 63rd with a 0.54 score) and “fundamental rights” (ranked 69th with a 0.55 score).
Hong Kong ranked 25th in “constraints in government’s power” in 2016, fell to 31st in 2020, then plummeted to 54th in 2022, and further tumbled to 63rd in 2025 and 2026.

The enactment of the National Security Law in Hong Kong on June 30, 2020, which empowered the Hong Kong government to shut down independent media outlets and NGOs, was the main driving force in the recent plunges.

Other factors included officials’ decision to rewrite electoral laws under the guiding principle of “patriots administering Hong Kong” in May 2021, the 2023 district council reform to restrict district councilors’ power and exclude oppositional figures, and the passage of domestic security law in March 2024 to outlaw acts including treason, espionage that harms the city, and incitement that provokes hatred.
Rights groups say all of these provisions have chilled civil society activity and encroached on citizens’ fundamental rights.

items.title: The Brazilian left’s quest to ‘tame’ Meta: A narrative of denouncement and resistance

s: Internet rights advocates and Lula da Silva campaigners challenge Meta’s alleged shadow banning
Over the years, Meta’s content moderation policies and governance practices have faced intense scrutiny and legal challenges over alleged political bias and a lack of transparency.

Since 2018, the Arab Center for Social Media Advancement (7amleh), a human rights organization advocating for Palestinian digital rights, has documented how Facebook’s (now Meta) moderation practices disproportionately affect Palestinian content.
In 2020, 7amleh launched a campaign challenging Facebook’s proposed hate speech policy, which considered “Zionist” a potential proxy for “Jew” or “Jewish.

More recently, in 2024, the organization collected 20 first-hand testimonies from Palestinian influencers, journalists, and media outlets documenting their experiences of Meta’s discriminatory content moderation practices.
In 2023, Human Rights Watch also reported “systemic online censorship” against voices in support of Palestine and Palestinian human rights,

In 2022, Tom Vandendriessche, a Belgian politician and Member of the European Parliament (MEP) representing the far-right Vlaams Belang (Flemish Interest) party, partially prevailed in a legal case against Meta concerning a shadow ban imposed on his account in 2021 after the company removed several posts alleging a breach of its Terms of Service (ToS) and Facebook Community Guidelines (FCG).

A Belgian court ordered the company to compensate the politician for financial and reputational damages, finding that its actions had significantly restricted his ability to engage in political discourse online and that Meta had failed to provide adequate transparency or effective avenues for redress.

In 2026, Meta has faced significant criticism in Brazil and internationally from internet rights watchdogs over political bias, algorithmic interference, and the selective suppression of content perceived as favoring far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro during the October 2026 Brazilian presidential election.

Using the slogan Meta não se meta (roughly, “Meta, stay out of it”), which plays on the Portuguese word meta, derived from the verb meter (“to get involved” or “to interfere”), internet rights defenders and current President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s followers and allies sought not only to expose alleged Meta’s shadow-banning practices during Brazil’s 2026 presidential election but also to mobilize Brazilians to demand a fairer digital space collectively.

In October 2026, during the Brazilian presidential runoff election campaign, a coalition of Brazilian civil society organizations, social movements, and digital rights advocacy groups, including CTRL+Z, Código Não Binário, ARTIGO 19 (Article 19 Brasil), Sleeping Giants Brasil, and others, launched the webpage naosemeta.com.br as part of their initiative to denounce electoral interference and algorithmic bias.

The site offered three ways for people to hold Meta accountable online: email Meta; message Meta’s General Director in Brazil on LinkedIn; and comment on Meta Ceo Mark Zuckerberg’s latest Instagram post.

It also shared a space for those wishing to join and sign a petition to the Superior Electoral Court and an extrajudicial notification, a formal written communication sent on October 19 to put Meta on notice and demand that it recognize the technical flaws in its advertising, moderation, and artificial intelligence (AI) systems, and the distribution and availability of user-generated content and campaign materials in Brazil — which these organizations claim disadvantaged, in particular, candidate Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

The online strategy to hold Meta accountable was accompanied by a protest in front of Meta’s offices on October 19, where participants called for respect for Brazil’s digital sovereignty, with the Homeless Workers Movement’s Technology Center among the loudest voices.
For those reclaiming digital sovereignty, the company’s actions stem from the relationship between U.S.

President Donald Trump and Brazil’s ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, father of Flávio Bolsonaro, and the influence the current U.S. administration has over big-tech owners — they consider Meta to be facilitating foreign interference.

items.title: In Kazakhstan, rural women are forming collectives to improve their livelihoods

s: Their most pressing challenge is solving the long-standing water shortage in the village
Participants of the project in Qyzylsay, Kazakhstan.
Photo by Nazgul Aidabossynova.
Used with permission.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South.
It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.
Women in the rural areas of Kazakhstan are among those most affected by climate change, energy deficit, and poor governance.

They bear the heavy burden of water shortages, especially in the southern parts of the country, where this problem is the most acute due to dense population, economic reliance on agriculture, and water losses related to outdated irrigation infrastructure.
In the village of Qyzylsay, located in the southern Jambyl region, the water shortage has become a major issue affecting the daily lives of women.
It forces them to spend multiple hours a day outside their homes to secure water for their households, gardens, and animals.
Their grueling work often goes unnoticed and unpaid, and their geographical remoteness places limits on access to information and government services, exacerbating their situation.

In 2026, Nazgul Aidabossynova, a local activist, implemented a project to help local women improve their livelihoods by training them to engage with the government more effectively and efficiently, calculate the cost of their labor and products, and mobilize collective efforts to solve community problems.
Global Voices conducted an email interview with Aidabossynova to learn more about her initiative.
The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.
Nazgul Aidabossynova (NA): I represent a community-based initiative led by rural women in Qyzylsay.

Our work focuses on supporting women who manage households, small farms, livestock, and care responsibilities, while also facing limited access to information, public services, and opportunities for civic participation.
We chose to participate in the Digital Sparks project because digital tools can make a direct, practical difference in women’s daily lives.
Many women already own smartphones, but previously used them mainly for calls and WhatsApp.

The project created an opportunity to turn these devices into tools for accessing eGov services, documenting community problems, managing farm and household responsibilities, protecting digital security, and communicating with local authorities.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?
NA: The key challenge is unreliable access to water in Qyzylsay.
Water often disappears from the pipes during the day, particularly in summer.
This affects gardens, livestock, household work, and the health and well-being of families.
The burden falls disproportionately on women.
They wake early to store water, carry water for household and agricultural needs, care for the livestock, and wait for irrigation turns.
Much of this work is unpaid, time-consuming, and rarely recognized.

Women also faced barriers in reporting water problems: they knew what was happening, but often lacked the knowledge, evidence, and confidence needed to raise concerns effectively with local institutions.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?
NA: The project delivered four practical training sessions for ten rural women.

The first one, titled “Your Phone is More Than WhatsApp: Smartphone as Your Household Assistant”, taught them how to use smartphone reminders, photo-diaries for farm and livestock work, eGov services, strong passwords, and basic digital-security practices.

In the second workshop, titled “Smart Water: When Your Garden Tells You It’s Thirsty”, participants learned about water rights, the responsibilities of relevant local authorities, and water-supply mapping using timestamped and GPS-tagged photographs.

items.title: When chatbots become ‘answer engines’: AI, geopolitics and truth

s: Hyrije Mehmeti presenting research report “The Chatbot Version of Truth” at Hibrid.info international expert conference held on 16 December 2025 in Prishtina, Kosovo.
Photo by Global Voices, CC BY 3.0.
This article by Hyrije Mehmeti combines and adapts material from the author's earlier work, including an article published in German by the European Journalism Observatory.
It draws on the 2025 ADS/Hibrid.info research report The Chatbot Version of Truth.
It is also part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “ Big Tech and Authoritarianism.
In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South.
You can support this coverage by donating here.
For many people today, asking a chatbot a question feels as natural as opening a search engine once did.
“Is Kosovo an independent state?
“What happened in Srebrenica?
“Is Crimea part of Ukraine or Russia?” — these are no longer questions reserved for history books, court rulings, or newsrooms.
They are typed into chat windows that respond in seconds, in fluent, confident language, often with the tone of an all-knowing guide.
That confidence is exactly what makes large language model (LLM) chatbots so attractive, and so risky at the same time.

Alongside social media platforms and online news outlets, AI chatbots are increasingly functioning as reference tools, offering summaries of complex political and historical subjects, often without users verifying the information they receive.
This shift matters particularly in regions such as the Western Balkans, where history, statehood and war legacies remain politically contested.
The way these issues are explained and framed is therefore not only a question of factual accuracy, but also of narrative influence.
LLMs are designed to generate text that sounds convincing.
They produce fluent and coherent responses, but these qualities do not guarantee verified truth.
If something reads clearly and authoritatively, it feels reliable.
Unlike traditional information sources, chatbots do not simply retrieve facts.
They also interpret, prioritise and frame information in ways shaped by their training data and the technological environments in which they operate.

In 2025, I led a research team at Action for Democratic Society/Hibrid.info that examined how three widely used AI chatbots responded to sensitive political and historical questions: ChatGPT (launched in the United States), DeepSeek Chat (launched in China), and Alice (launched in Russia).

The study, titled “ The Chatbot Version of Truth,” analysed what kind of “truth” these systems produce when people use them as shortcut information sources for specific topics concerning Kosovo, critical issues related to the Western Balkans (WB) and global comparative topics.

The team developed 100 standardised prompts covering issues such as the independence of Kosovo, the war legacy, international recognition, EU integration of West Balkan countries, memory politics, regional disputes, and global comparative questions like Crimea, Cyprus, or other contested territories.
A separate account was created in each chatbot for every thematic area, and each prompt was entered separately into a new chat, to avoid previous answers influencing the next one.
The responses were then checked for factual accuracy and compared for semantic similarity.
Semi-structured interviews with experts were also conducted, which were used to verify and interpret the experimental findings.
Initially, the results suggested a positive picture: most answers were broadly accurate, with ChatGPT and DeepSeek Chat demonstrating the highest and most consistent accuracy.
However, both systems still produced inaccuracies, elements of hallucination, and interpretive variations.
Alice showed a weaker performance, with the highest number of refusals to answer, thematic evasions, and ideological deviations, particularly on politically sensitive topics.
Performance of the chatbots in the 100 tested prompts by accuracy categories.
Graph by hibrid.info, used with permission.
One of the clearest findings was that none of the tested systems could be considered a fully neutral or consistently reliable reference point for geopolitical issues.

items.title: How one Haitian entrepreneur found success by supporting all things local

s: REB Lokal founder Rébetha Charles stands with a jar of peanut butter ( manba lokal).
Photo courtesy of Rébetha Charles, used with permission.

For several decades, due to the significant reduction of tariff barriers on foreign goods — particularly those from the United States and the Dominican Republic — Haiti has depended heavily on imported products for local consumption.

The arrangement began under various structural adjustment programmes that were initiated between 1994 and 1995, through agreements between the Haitian government and international financial institutions like the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank.

Since then, imports have practically invaded the Haitian market, creating inequitable competition for local farmers who rely on subsistence agriculture and traditional, rudimentary equipment, and significantly weakening national production.

Complicating the economic reality is Haiti’s ongoing struggle with gang violence, political instability, and the absence of adequate infrastructure; yet, many Haitians continue to take on ambitious initiatives.
Take Rébetha Charles, a 38-year-old woman entrepreneur.

Originally from Jérémie, Charles studied agronomy, works in the Grand’Anse department in Haiti’s southern region, of which Jérémie is the capital, and created an agri-food enterprise called REB Lokal.
Rébetha Charles.
Photo courtesy of Rébetha Charles, used with permission.
REB is a short form of her name; Lokal speaks to the pride inherent in making local products.
Her company buys products from small farmers and, in its small manufacturing plant, transforms these local harvests into healthy, sustainable, tasty products.
In a WhatsApp interview, Charles says she is proud of a few key things.
First, her company adds value.

Through a manufacturing process that produces authentic, nutritious, and 100 percent local products, farmers have a much better guarantee of not losing their crops, whereas before, various obstacles, including spoilage, prevented them from selling their produce at market.

Charles explains that the REB Lokal project is an enterprise that transforms local agricultural products: “We work with a supplier network of almost 2,000 people, including agricultural producers and small traders.
We have more than 20 employees, so we work every day to grow the project even more.”

Second, Charles is pleased with the company’s focus on providing safe, fresh food that meets modern food processing standards — its approach places value on Haitian culinary traditions to preserve the natural taste and nutritional value of local ingredients.
Finally, REB Lokal makes a point of avoiding chemical additives and artificial ingredients, as part of its commitment to providing consumers with healthy, accessible, community-friendly food.
Charles didn’t initially see herself as an entrepreneur.
Before she decided to enter the agro business, she was working at an international humanitarian organisation, but resigned because of a culture — fairly common in Haiti — of sexual harassment.
“In Haiti,” she stresses, “a woman’s life is not easy when it comes to work.
Instead of competence, sometimes there are other things they ask from us.

Sometimes, some of us stand up and say, ‘No, we do not agree,’ because we went to school just like everyone else, got experience where we needed — and after that, there are things we choose not to do.”
That professional environment left her with “such a disgust for work” that, even though she had been offered other opportunities in bigger organisations, she decided to put everything on pause.
Charles finally submitted her resignation letter on August 31, 2020, and launched the REB Lokal project the very next day.
Workers packaging chocolate balls at the factory.
Photo courtesy of Rébetha Charles, used with permission.

items.title: How the streets and a social media army led Lula to a historic win in Brazil

s: For the first time in the country, a candidate managed to turn the results in the run-off
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva waves Brazil’s flag surrounded by a crowd of supporters in São Paulo, during the 2026 election campaign.
Photo by Ricardo Stuckert/Lula Oficial on Flickr ( CC BY-SA 4.0 ).

On April 7, 2018, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who had been president of Brazil twice, waited in the building of the Metalworkers’ Union, in São Bernardo do Campo, São Paulo state, where his political life started in the 1970s, to be arrested by the Federal Police following convictions for corruption and money laundering.
Gilberto Carvalho, one of his oldest allies, later recalled that they hoped for a crowd of 50,000, but only 10,000 people waited outside.
Lula looked through the window, grabbed his arm, and said, “Gilbertinho, we go to war with the soldiers we have.”
Eight years and six months after that day, on October 25, 2026, Lula was elected president of Brazil for the fourth time, supported by millions of people in the streets and an army of his own online.
The convictions against him were later annulled by the Federal Supreme Court (STF), which ruled that the lower federal court lacked jurisdiction and was biased.
Lula spent 580 days in prison.
His latest victory was also the first time a candidate was elected after losing the first round in Brazil.
In 20 days, Lula, a member of the Workers‘ Party, managed to turn Flavio Bolsonaro’s advantage of 2.2 million votes into a win by a 4.4 million-vote difference.
As the BBC explained, both candidates increased their votes in the second round, in an election with the lowest abstention rate since 2006.
The leftist’s victory came from five million new voters, with a drop in absences, blank and nulled votes, says UOL news portal.
Also, it left the world in awe, wondering just how he did it.
Lula gathered the support of massive crowds in the streets and an online army led by federal deputy André Janones, who poses with him during a livestream.
Photos by Ricardo Stuckert/Lula Oficial on Flickr.
Collage by Global Voices on Canva Pro.

Lula reset his campaign in the second round, bringing new people into his team and riding on the so-called R-factor — ruas e redes, Portuguese for “streets and networks” — which started organically and was embraced by his team.

On October 5, while many were dispirited by the first-round results, students from UFF (Fluminense Federal University) took to the streets in the city of Niterói, Rio de Janeiro state, in a pro-Lula act that spread nationally in the following weeks.

Lula’s official events also left the stage used in the first round and instead moved to the streets for massive marches, during which he led the crowds from a truck and talked to supporters about his proposals, his own history, and the threats presented by his opponent, all while waving Brazil’s flag.
On October 7, federal deputy André Janones posted about an initiative that would hack social media and contribute to turning the election around.

On X, Janones wrote that he had recruited 1.5 million people for a WhatsApp channel, inviting more to join and saying: “This is the ONLY way of bursting the bubble, since Meta only organically delivers right-leaning content.
After threats of being taken down by the electoral court, by voting day, the public channel had 11 million people.

items.title: A digital publication sheds light on Turkey’s prison system

s: ‘No independent body regularly monitored developments in prisons and communicat’d this information to the public using data.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South.
It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

In Turkey, a team of two journalists and human rights activists launched a digital publication, Prison Agenda, to report on what is happening inside the country’s prisons and prison system, information that is often hidden from the Turkish public and the world.
As the Nordic Monitor noted in 2025, Turkey’s prison population has reached an unprecedented level.
Citing figures from the Directorate General of Prisons and Houses of Detention, the website states that as of September 1, 2025, Turkish prisons hold 419,194 individuals.
This includes 356,710 convicted prisoners and 62,484 people in pretrial detention.
The figure exceeds the official capacity of 295,000 and places immense strain on the country’s penal system.

Le Monde also wrote in 2026 that a commissioned report on prison conditions among Council of Europe member states showed that France and Turkey each had 131 inmates for every 100 places, making them the two most overcrowded prison systems.
For the relatives of people in prison, as well as for national and international human rights organizations and agencies, the information provided by the Prison Agenda publication can be vital.
A similar organization — Russia Behind Bars — used to work in Russia.

While it did not function exclusively as a publication, it received letters from prisoners and their relatives, published news about torture or other human rights violations, and reported how the prison population had been drafted, in the hundreds of thousands, to fight Russia’s war with Ukraine.
Unfortunately, it had to shut down its work within Russia because of the regime’s prosecution, but it continues to inform from abroad.

Civil society organizations, such as the publication about Prisons and Prisoners, are vital to the country and the world; they need to continue their important work within one of the most opaque systems in the world.
Global Voices interviewed one of Prison Agenda’s founder, Ahmet Kavruk, by email.
GV: Please tell us about your organization, and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Spark project?
Ahmet Kavruk ( AK): Prison Agenda is a digital publication that covers data on Turkey’s prisons, legislative changes relating to prisons, and human rights violations within them.
It is guided by an independent, rights-focused approach to journalism.
We launched in January 2026.

Our aim is to make the often complicated and scattered information about prisons more accessible to the public by presenting it in a clear and understandable way, and to highlight the human stories behind the statistics.
Shortly after launching in January, we reached a crossroads.

We could either continue as a passion project, publishing solely in Turkish, which would be easier to sustain, but would not fulfil our potential, or evolve into a publishing model that would require more intensive work, but enable us to reach a wider audience.
It was precisely at this decision-making stage that we came across the Digital Spark call for proposals.
It was one of the few support programmes capable of creating space for initiatives working in specific and often overlooked fields, such as prisons.
We, therefore, drew up a plan and, should we be accepted into Digital Sparks, began to focus on the question, ‘How can we grow the Prison Agenda?’

items.title: In Albania, rural youth are campaigning to solve local environmental problems

s: Their petition to the authorities has already gathered over 500 signatures
DigiAction picnic held in Lozhan village, Albania.
Photo by Qendra KAZUS.
Used with permission.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South.
It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.
In rural parts of Albania, youth are seldom mobilized to help solve local environmental and other problems in their communities, although they, too, are affected by them.
This has been the case in the eastern Korce region as well, which was hit by heavy rainfall and subsequent devastating floods in November 2025.

In the Maliq municipality, one of the affected areas, the situation was worsened by improper disposal of waste that blocked drainage channels, including the Devoll River, which flows through the area.
Illegal waste disposal has obstructed the river’s infrastructure and contributed to widespread flooding.
Despite efforts by the authorities to improve waste management and clean up the river, the situation has remained dire.
Waste accumulated at the Devoll River Bridge in Maliq, Albania.
Photo from November 21, 2025 by Qendra KAZUS.
Used with permission.
In 2026, a local non-governmental organization (NGO), Qendra KAZUS, recruited and trained local youth to help solve this long-standing issue by turning them into environmental advocates.

Global Voices conducted an email interview with Dhorjela Cela, the group’s executive director, to learn about how Qendra KAZUS implemented a project that brought together youth, digital democracy, environmental challenges, and advocacy.
The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.
Dhorjela Cule (DC): Qendra KAZUS was founded in 2024 and focuses on young people’s activism and engagement.
Our team brings together journalists, photojournalists, and education specialists with years of experience in media, law, and mentoring.

Our mission is to strengthen democracy and the rule of law through youth advocacy and to raise awareness around preserving cultural heritage, protecting the environment, and building capacity in ICT and media.
As a young organization, our work relied mainly on small activities and projects.
Digital Sparks gave us the opportunity to prioritize digital advocacy.
We saw a chance to give young people in rural areas and cities tools they use every day — their phones and social media — and turn them into instruments of civic participation and accountability.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?
DC: The Devoll River in the eastern Korça region is facing a serious environmental situation.
Plastic pollution, inert waste, agricultural waste, and other debris accumulate along the riverbanks.

During winter floods, high river flows expose and spread this waste, blocking drainage canals, and water overflows from the riverbed into agricultural land and residential areas, damaging soil health, livelihoods, and the local ecosystem.
In the villages of Lozhan and Pojan, the waste is considerable, and local authorities seem to have their hands tied in finding a solution.
What worried us most was that young people from rural areas, whose families depend on agriculture and are directly affected, were excluded from the search for solutions.
They had phones and strong opinions, but no channel to turn them into public pressure.
We wanted to show that the right to a clean environment is something young people can demand with evidence and a collective voice.
Waste on the banks of the Devoll River in Pojan from May 2026.
Photo by Qendra KAZUS.
Used with permission.

items.title: A Myanmar journalist’s reflection: ‘When other people’s pain becomes part of you’

s: An Exile Hub fellow shares their personal experiences and reflections
Exile Hub is one of Global Voices’ partners in Southeast Asia, emerging in response to the 2021 coup in Myanmar, and focusing on empowering journalists and human rights defenders.
This article by a fellow of Exile Hub was published on August 15, 2026, and an edited version is republished under a content partnership agreement.
I have asked myself that question more times than I can count.
When I first entered journalism as a young person, I was full of energy, conviction, and dreams.
I believed journalism was a way to uncover the truth and to make sure people’s voices were heard.
Four years later, I began to realize that somewhere along the way, I was slowly losing parts of myself.
When I was 19, I never imagined that the career I chose would become both my livelihood and one of the reasons the road home would feel so far away.
In the early days of the 2021 revolution in Myanmar, I took part in protests.
As the security situation deteriorated, I had to leave home.
Eventually, I found myself in Mae Sot, a small town along the Thai–Myanmar border.
There, I was fortunate to have the opportunity to study journalism for free.
I had loved writing since I was young.
I started with short news pieces, then moved on to feature stories and video reporting, and eventually became a news presenter.
I was proud to call myself a journalist.
I was so proud, in fact, that I never used a pen name.
I reported under my real name.
One of the first lessons I learned in journalism was simple: don’t put your own emotions into the story.
But over time, I learned something else.
Journalists are human too.
Sometimes I would call a source for an interview and listen as they described what had happened to them.
Their pain would stay with me.
My responsibility was to listen carefully and then find the words to make their experiences visible to others.
But sometimes, carrying their stories felt like carrying the pain twice.
After some interviews, I would put down my phone, open my laptop, and stare at the screen.
No words would come.
I remember once speaking with a source just before mealtime.
My stomach told me I was hungry, but after hearing their story, there was a heaviness in my chest, and I could not eat.
As these experiences accumulated, something began to change.
I could finish an interview and immediately continue with the next task.
But it wasn’t because the stories no longer affected me.
And that numbness slowly changed me without my realizing it.
I became tired more easily.
I became irritable.
I overthought things.
My mood sank, and even my relationships with other people began to suffer.
On the days when I picked up my camera bag, carried my tripod, and went out into the field, some of that exhaustion disappeared.
Walking along windy roads, meeting people and listening to their lives, I would suddenly remember:
COVID-19 and Myanmar’s political upheaval interrupted my education.
Journalism became my livelihood, and surviving from one day to the next left little space to think seriously about my own future.
Eventually, one question began following me almost every day: What will become of me?
At the same time, media organizations were losing funding.
Programs were closing.
Journalists were losing their jobs.
When one of the programs I worked for ended, I became unemployed for around seven months.
I told myself that if I could not find another job in journalism within a little over a year, I would change careers completely.
Fortunately, I eventually found my way back, working again as both a reporter and news presenter.

items.title: Bangladesh weighs tougher cyber law as AI-generated abuse targets women

s: State surveillance and policing of online expression have a long history in the country
Bangladesh is revising its cyber law to tackle AI-generated images, and the draft has triggered a furious debate over how much the state should police speech online.
The ICT Division published the draft Cyber Protection (Amendment) Act for public comment in mid-September.
It is now with a five-member cabinet committee led by Posts, Telecommunications and ICT Minister Faqir Mahbub Anam.
In a discussion reported on October 19, media figures, legal analysts, and civil society representatives called for the most contested clauses to be removed.
The push follows a campaign season crowded with synthetic media.
Global Voices previously reported on a study that identified 72 AI-manipulated items that gained traction between December 2025 and the February 12, 2026 election.
Synthetic images of political figures were the most common tactic, alongside doctored news-channel graphics.
The Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), which went on to win, was the most frequent target, with 47 cases.
State surveillance and policing of online expression have a long history.
Section 57 of the Information and Communication Technology (ICT) Act of 2006 punished online content seen as defamatory, hurtful to religious sentiment, or damaging to the state’s image.
A 2013 amendment toughened it, with sentences of up to 14 years.
Journalists and ordinary social media users were among those charged under it.
After years of protest, the government promised to scrap Section 57.
Yet when the Digital Security Act (DSA) was signed into law in October 2018, the same offenses reappeared in sections 25, 28, 29 and 31.
By 2023, the law minister had told parliament that 7,001 cases had been filed under it.
The writer Mushtaq Ahmed died in custody in 2021 after ten months in jail under the DSA, which led to protests at home and abroad.
The Awami League government replaced the DSA with the Cyber Security Act in 2023, but Amnesty International said it repackaged almost all of the DSA’s repressive features.
After the July 2024 uprising, the interim government scrapped nine sections through a new Cyber Security Ordinance in 2025.
Rights groups say hundreds of cases from earlier years are still pending.
Women in politics faced a particular kind of attack.

A Daily Star analysis of AI content before the vote found that pro-Awami League pages targeted female leaders of the National Citizen Party (NCP) with fabricated images that hinted at moral and sexual impropriety.
After the election, a Prothom Alo fact-check found AI-generated images and invented statements aimed at nominees for reserved women's seats.
Tanvir Mahatab Abir of Rumor Scanner told the paper that visible women, especially in politics, are frequent targets of disinformation.
Not all of it is political.

Data from the Daily Star shows that Facebook pages used deepfake videos of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and his family, including his daughter Zaima Rahman, to promote fake “Family Card” offers in exchange for likes and follows.
Among 52 posts analyzed, 13 featured Zaima.
One page administrator told the fact-checking outlet Dismislab that the aim was to gain followers quickly and sell the pages.
In such cases, for many creators of synthetic content, monetization metrics on social platforms often serve as a primary driver alongside political motives.
For ordinary women, the damage can last much longer.
Farzana Sithi, a student activist known for her role in the historic student-led uprising in 2024, was targeted by a fake Facebook profile that Dismislab investigated in March 2025.
Of 166 videos and reels posted between December 13, 2024, and March 17, 2025, 133 were AI-generated deepfakes.
They placed her face on videos of two Indian content creators.
The five most-viewed clips drew more than 4.1 million views, and the account was monetized through Facebook's Stars feature.

items.title: Opposition leader Tarique Rahman returns to Bangladesh after 17 years

s: Tarique Rahman, the acting chairman of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) returned to Bangladesh on December 25, 2025, landing in Dhaka after 17 years in self-imposed exile in London.
His arrival marks a significant development in the country's political landscape following the ouster of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina in August 2024.
Rahman is the son of Khaleda Zia, the official chairperson of the party and former Prime Minister of Bangladesh.
Upon landing at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka, Rahman was greeted by thousands of Bangladesh Nationalist Party supporters amid tight security.

Accompanied by his wife, Zubaida Rahman, and daughter, Zaima Rahman, he addressed a rally, emphasizing national unity, inclusivity across religious lines, and the vision of a democratic and economically strong Bangladesh.
He drew parallels to the country's 1971 war of independence.
Rahman, aged 60, left Bangladesh in 2008 for medical treatment after being released on bail following 18 months in detention during the military-backed government's rule from 2006 to 2008.
He was convicted in absentia of charges including corruption, money laundering, and involvement in a 2004 grenade attack on a political rally for his political rival, Sheikh Hasina.
These convictions were overturned or stayed after Hasina's government's fall.
His return comes amid preparations for general elections scheduled for early 2026, under an interim government led by Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus.
The elections follow a student-led uprising in 2024 that resulted in Hasina's removal and her subsequent flight to India.
The protests, initially sparked by opposition to a job quota system, escalated into broader anti-government demonstrations, leading to an estimated 1,400 deaths according to United Nations figures.
Hasina has since been sentenced to death in absentia for crimes against humanity related to the crackdown.
According to a December poll by the International Republican Institute, the BNP is the frontrunner for the election with 30 percent support.
The party has recently distanced itself from allies like Jamaat-e-Islami to adopt a more centrist approach.
However, challenges remain, including integrating party factions, maintaining law and order, and addressing potential unrest from Awami League supporters.
The Awami League was not allowed to participate in the elections.
Rahman's mother, Khaleda Zia, 80, is hospitalised in critical condition since November 2025.
She was the BNP's acting chairman since 2018 and was jailed most of the times during Hasina's administration.

items.title: United States capture Venezuelan president, Nicolás Maduro

s: The president of Venezuela, Nicolás Maduro, has been captured by the United States on Saturday at around 3 am UTC-4, according to a post by US president Donald Trump on social media.
Trump has told reporters Maduro had been “in a house that was more like a fortress”, in the country’s capital, Caracas.
Trump justified this action by claiming that Maduro is the leader of the Cartel de los Soles, and pushing illegal immigration of dangerous individuals in the United States.
Yván Gil Pinto, Venezuela’s foreign minister, said the country has requested a United Nations Security Council meeting to be held after the attack.
The BBC reports airstrikes in Caracas targeting La Carlota, an airbase and Fort Tiuna, a military base where the United States suspected Maduro to be located, and in other locations.
According to local authorities there has been civilian deaths and injuries, but the exact numbers are still unknown.
It was also reported by the BBC that the operation was orchestrated by a {CIA infiltration of the Venezuelan government.
France 24 reported that the CIA had been monitoring his “every movement since August”, despite Maduro’s efforts to change location regularly.
It was also reported that the operation involved more than 150 military aircraft, including one helicopter that was to capture Maduro.

According to the United States authorities, the Delta Force special operation force, arrived at Maduro’s location at “2:01 a.m. local time” and were able to capture him before he could get into his solid steel safe room (sources contradict however, on his exact location at that point.
Some sources reported that Trump said Maduro was almost in his safe room whilst others said he was sleeping in his bed).
They then relocated the “indicted persons” on a ship after crossing the coastline of Venezuela at 3:29 am.

Trump later revealed that Maduro’s wife, Cilia Flores, was also captured, and both were on board the USS Iwo Jima (LHD-7) with destination the southern district of New York, ultimately to be prosecuted.

Attorney General Pam Bondi was quoted by the BBC saying “[he will] face the full wrath of American justice on American soil in American courts” and, according to CNN, announced an indictment for leading “state‐sponsored gangs” and supporting drug trafficking.
Venezuelan authorities also reported other strikes, said to be made with the intent of seizing their oil and minerals, and have declared national emergency.
They, along with Cuba, Colombia, Iran and Russia, have denounced the action as a “serious military aggression”.
Argentine’s president, Javier Milei supported the action.
Venezuela’s vice‐president, Delcy Rodríguez called for Maduro and his wife to be released, saying the operation violated the country’s territorial integrity.
The BBC stated that these strikes follow a string of more than 30 strikes on Venezuelan vessels, and a strike on a “dock area” in Maracaibo, resulting in the death of more than 110 people.
The Trump administration stated that it is engaging in “non‐international armed conflict with […] alleged drug traffickers”.
According to the BBC, legal experts doubt the legality of these actions, saying the strikes are not against "lawful military targets".
According to CNN, Trump also justified not advising Congress before the operation to avoid a "leak", which drew criticisms from Democratic lawmakers.

After the capture, the US Justice Department unsealed an indictment against Maduro in which Maduro and others were charged with “conspiracy to commit narco‐terrorism and conspiracy to import cocaine”.

According to the BBC, Maduro has denied this and has said before that Trump’s actual goal is to get access to Venezuela’s oil reserves, as indicated by the United States’ confiscation of several oil tankers.

items.title: Kyiv street to be named for former Ukrainian parliament chairman Andriy Parubiy, killed in Lviv

s: A street in Kyiv will be named after the former Speaker of the Parliament Andriy Parubiy, killed in Lviv.
The initiative to commemorate the prominent Ukrainian politician was supported by 57% of participants in a public poll on "Kyiv Digital" application.
On January 1, Maryna Poroshenko, the leader of “European Solidarity”, announced the street name in the Kyiv City Council and on Facebook.
As the result, a section along Mariinsky Park – from Hrushevskoho Street to Parkova Road – will bear the politician's name, named "Andrei Parubia Street".
In December, former President of Ukraine and head of the European Solidarity party Petro Poroshenko asked the residents of Kyiv to support the vote to name the street after Parubiy.
The street had no name at the time of the proposal.
"This place is significant for our team and for Andriy himself — a significant part of his journey is connected with it," Poroshenko said.
On October 1, 2025, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed a decree awarding Parubiy the title of Hero of Ukraine.

A petition to award the title of Hero of Ukraine to Parubiy was registered on the presidential website on September 2, gaining 25,000 signatures, which was necessary for the proposal to be considered by President.
The Verkhovna Rada, the Ukrainian parliament, also supported the request.
Parubiy was among several people who were conferred Heroes of Ukraine.
Others were writer Volodymyr Vakulenko and student and footballer Stepan Chubenko.
Poroshenko lauded the decision, recalling that "Parubiy dedicated his entire life to serving Ukraine".
Andriy Parubiy, 54, who served as the Chairman of Verkhovna Rada from 14 April 2016 to 29 August 2019, was shot and killed in Lviv on 30 August 2025.
He died at the scene from injuries.
The killing happened amid the Russian invasion, which started in 2022.
The shooter managed to escape.
Later, Ukrainian authorities detained a suspect, and allege there is a Russian link to the killing.
Parubiy was an active participant of Euromaidan.
He also served as Secretary of the National Security and Defence Council of Ukraine from February till August 2014.
The suspected killer of Ukrainian lawmaker Andriy Parubiy admitted on 2 September his role in the killing.
He claimed to have comitted the crime in an act of "revenge" against the country’s authorities.
He denied having worked with Russian special services.

items.title: "I came to be the manager ... not the coach": Manchester United fire head coach Ruben Amorim

s: On Monday, Manchester United football team fired its coach Ruben Amorim after fourteen months in the role.
Amorim had met with Omar Berrada, chief executive officer of the team, and Jason Wilcox, the team's director of football, on Friday morning.
While discussing his preferred 3-4-3 style, the conversation reportedly quickly spiraled out of control, resulting in Amorim losing his job.
Manchester United announced the news of the dismissal at around 10 a.m. on Monday.
After the team drawing against Leeds F.C.
1-1, the coach had said at a press conference that he came to be "the manager, not the coach" and said Wilcox should "do his job".
Wilcox intended the meeting to focus on the recent draw.

Manchester United was sixth in the Premier League, almost not classifying for the Champions League, less than four points ahead of Sunderland A.F.C., Everton F.C., Fulham F.C., Brighton & Hove Albion F.C., Newcastle United and Brentford F.C., a precarious position, El Pais reported.
Former Manchester United captain Gary Neville communicated to Sky Sports News that he expected better performance, saying he "thought they'd get through another couple of weeks."

items.title: Homeland Security says Minneapolis woman shot by ICE officer dies

s: The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) reported Wednesday that a woman shot by a U.S.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer in Minneapolis has died.
Homeland Security officials have described the shooting as an act of self-defense, while Minnesota governor Tim Walz and Minneapolis mayor Jacob Frey have pushed back on this account.

DHS spokesperson Tricia McLaughlin stated that the shooting occurred when ICE officers fired "defensive shots" in response to the woman "attempting to run over our law enforcement officers" with her vehicle.
Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem said the woman’s conduct was "an act of domestic terrorism."
The incident was under active investigation, with the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension (BCA) and the FBI taking over the case.
Walz said the state was working to learn more and asked residents to remain calm, while protest activity continued at the scene and a substantial law-enforcement presence remained in the area.
According to ABC News, Jacob Frey, the mayor of Minneapolis, said in a statement that he was aware of the shooting and urged the agency to depart the city at once.
On social media, he stated the involvement of federal immigration officers was "causing chaos in our city.
He added that the city is "demanding ICE to leave the city immediately," and said officials "stand rock solid with our immigrant and refugee communities.
In a news conference, he disputed the account that the woman's vehicle was weaponized against the agent.

items.title: Roblox player uncovers cheating, awarded Guinness World Record

s: In early January, international media reported that Quinten Delaere, an 18-year-old, had been officially recognized by Guinness World Records after exposing cheating on the Roblox platform.
Delaere, known online as 'kannotlogin', used data analysis to demonstrate that the top times on the global leaderboard were achieved using illegal scripts.
Delaere was competing in a speed-running event for the game Ultimate Easy Obby.
The event was an official collaboration between Roblox and Guinness World Records.
Players had to complete a digital obstacle course as fast as possible.
According to JV, after weeks of practice, Delaere posted a time of 5 minutes and 48.96 seconds.
Before the competition closed, three unknown accounts posted times around 5 minutes and 42 seconds.
JV reported that Delaere, posting on Reddit, believed the times were humanly impossible.
Delaere conducted a digital forensic analysis and compiled a report alleging that the new records were fraudulent.
The report cited three technical points.
First, the analysis pointed to the timestamps of the badges earned by the rival accounts.
The data showed that badges were unlocked in a non-chronological order.
Delaere’s report described the non-chronological order as consistent with the use of teleportation scripts in a normally linear course.
Second, the top accounts were missing specific digital items in their inventory.
Players who cross the finish line automatically receive a 'digital receipt' (an in-game item).
The suspect accounts lacked this item.
According to Kotaku, Delaere argued that "this proved he never actually touched the finish line trigger; he likely teleported a coordinate script to the end-game lobby."
PCGamesN reported that Delaere’s investigation found expired items in the players’ inventories.
Delaere also submitted a frame-by-frame video analysis of his own run to calculate the theoretical maximum speed, arguing that the rival times were mathematically unachievable.
"I took my best run and calculated the theoretical maximum time save possible (perfect pixels, zero drag).
Even with a TAS (Tool-Assisted Speedrun) level of perfection, the times the cheaters posted were mathematically impossible within the game’s physics engine."
Delaere submitted his findings to the Guinness World Records headquarters in London.
MeriStation reported that, after an internal review, the organization concluded Delaere was correct, disqualified the other accounts, and awarded him the official world record.
The challenged times were removed from the database.
The time set by Delaere was officially recognized as the new world record.

items.title: Grateful Dead rhythm guitarist Bob Weir dies, aged 78

s: On Saturday, the family of American musician and songwriter Bob Weir announced that he had died surrounded by loved ones.
The former guitarist and vocalist of the rock band Grateful Dead was 78.
His family announced his death via Instagram, noting that he had recently fought a cancer diagnosis but died due to "underlying lung issues".
The announcement did not specify the date of Weir's death.

Weir played rhythm guitar and sang with American psychedelic rock band the Grateful Dead for decades, and also wrote some of their songs, including the hit "Sugar Magnolia", a staple of Grateful Dead concerts.
He also had a long solo career, making various groups with fellow Grateful Dead alumni, and playing live until months before his death.

Weir was born Robert Hall Parber on October 16, 1947, in San Francisco, California, and grew up in the San Francisco Bay Area, spending some time going to school in Colorado, where he met future Grateful Dead member John Perry Barlow.
Weir started playing guitar at age 13 and gravitated to a local bluegrass scene, where he first encountered Jerry Garcia playing banjo.
On December 31, 1965, Garcia and Weir agreed to form their own group called Mother McCree's Uptown Jug Champions, which evolved into the Grateful Dead.
Weir played rhythm guitar, and sang for the group, for decades.

He also explored a solo career and variety of other groups outside of the Grateful Dead starting in the 1970s, including Kingfish, Bobby and the Midnites, RatDog, Furthur, The Other Ones, The Dead, Wolf Bros, and Dead & Company.
All groups featured fellow Grateful Dead collaborators and explored genres from country rock to jam band to jazz-influenced roots rock with a basis in blues and country.

His vocal contributions were mostly only harmonies and as a backup singer, but he took lead on several tracks, including Grateful Dead anthem "Truckin'", a song noted by the Library of Congress as a national treasure in 1997.

Outside of musical performance, Weir has also established Tamalpais Research Institute, a virtual performance platform, and was active in politics, advocating for several causes, including environmentalism, poverty relief, and issues related to the arts.
He had stayed active in the Bay Area music scene, performing live with local musicians and co-owning the venue Sweetwater Music Hall in Mill Valley, California.
He is survived by wife Natascha and daughters Chloe and Monet, as well as other family.

items.title: Boy retrieves Nintendo Switch locked away in gun safe, and shoots his father

s: On January 13, the night of his 11th birthday, a boy allegedly shot his father with a gun retrieved from a gun safe in the family's home in Duncannon Borough, Pennsylvania.
According to court documents, the boy told investigators he became mad after his father told him to go to bed.
Police charged the boy with criminal homicide.
The court has refused bail.
The boy was placed in Perry County Prison, and an initial court hearing was scheduled for January 22, according to a criminal docket.
According to court documents, the mother was asleep until the gunshot woke her.
When state police arrived at the home, the boy was heard shouting "Daddy's dead" and was overheard telling his mother, "I killed Daddy."
Police arrived on scene around 3:20 a.m.
Eastern Standard Time (08:20 UTC).
According to the affidavit, the boy told the police that he did not think about what would happen after the shot, saying he was "mad and did not think about that."

According to court documents, the boy told investigators he found a key to the gun safe in a drawer and unlocked the safe in an attempt to get back his Nintendo Switch, then loaded the gun and shot his father.
The Nintendo Switch had been placed in a gun safe located in the parents' bedroom.
The parents adopted the boy in 2018, according to a report by the New York Post.

items.title: Bruce Gallanter interviews Elliott Sharp, Joe Fonda at Downtown Music Gallery event

s: On January 12, Downtown Music Gallery in New York City hosted a public reading and discussion featuring Elliott Sharp and Joe Fonda, followed by their first-ever live performance together as a duo.
The event also included extended, in-person interviews conducted by Bruce Gallanter focused on the artists’ recently published books.
Sharp read first from his new book, Feedback: Translations from the IrRational, and was then interviewed by Gallanter.
Fonda then discussed passages from his new book, My Life in the World of Music.
After these talks, Sharp and Fonda, who have known each other since 1978, performed together using a variety of extended techniques.
Sharp played his electroacoustic guitar through an amplifier, while Fonda played acoustic contrabass with no amplification.
Note: This interview has been edited for clarity.
((Bruce Gallanter)) : Elliott, I have a few questions for you.
((Elliott Sharp)) : Okay, if we have time.
((Gallanter)) Yeah.
When did you pick up the guitar?
((Gallanter)) And you would listen to mostly rock music at that point?
((Sharp)) Yeah, and classical music.
I played classical piano as a kid and classical clarinet after that when I was eight, when the piano gave me asthma (in my interpretation) that nearly killed me.
So I played clarinet, then I got an electric guitar, and that was it.
The clarinet went by the wayside.

Also, I got kicked out of wind ensemble and marching band because I came back from a summer residency after my junior year with long hair and a beard, and Al Renino, the band director, would have none of that.
((Gallanter)) When you first started playing, were you playing kind of blues rock stuff at the beginning?

((Sharp)) Well, making psychedelic noise, I was very inspired by readings I was doing in Cage, I was an electronics geek, so I was building my own circuits and experimenting with tape delays and building ring modulators and fuzz, so I was making a lot of noise... and trying to learn Jeff Beck's guitar playing from the Yardbirds records and then Jimi Hendrix.
I mean, Jeff Beck's playing, at least I could find the notes.
With Hendrix, it was beyond me at first, it was just so sonic, you know, but yeah, and a lot of blues, country blues, playing a lot of slide.
((Gallanter)) So you played in blues rock bands?
((Sharp)) Yeah.
I was playing, the first blues band I was in was called the MFBB, the MotherFucking Blues Band, and I was playing bass in that.
((Sharp)) That was '68, '69 when I was still in high school.
I started playing guitar and pedal steel in bands in Ithaca in 1970 when I was at Cornell.
((Gallanter)) OK.
That's where you went to school first?

((Gallanter)) So you've had I mean, I know that most people think of you more as avant-garde kind of noisemaker, even with the guitar and the other instruments that you play, but it seems that you've always had that blues thing.
((Sharp)) Yeah, blues.
And I went for a long period of playing bebop and studying with Roswell Rudd.
But I'll still do gigs occasionally, playing like for a party, playing some blues or jazz or funk tunes, and people come and say, well, I didn't know you actually knew how to play guitar.
((Gallanter)) Somebody said the same thing today when we had on that Terraplane CD.
They said, this is Elliott Sharp?
He plays the blues?
I said, he plays the blues really well, and he's obviously studied it, because you've been doing records of that, starting with that Hoosegow record.

items.title: White House deletes Truth Social post portraying Obamas as apes

s: The White House has deleted a post on Donald Trump's social media account containing a video portraying former United States President Barack Obama and his wife Michelle Obama as apes.
The video triggered a backlash from American politicians, including from Trump's own Republican Party.
After initially defending the post, the White House removed the post from Trump's account in response to backlash, according to the BBC.
A White House official stated that a staff member had mistakenly posted the video.
Trump himself has stated that he did not see the full video prior to it being posted and according to ABC News Australia, he refused to apologize, stating "I didn't make a mistake.
I mean, I give - I look at a lot - thousands of things."
Senator Tim Scott, who is both African American and a Republican, referred to the video as "the most racist thing I've ever seen out of this White House."
The video, which lasts 62 seconds, used the song The Lion Sleeps Tonight as background music and references allegations of electoral fraud in the 2020 United States presidential election.

In addition to the Obamas, it portrays various other Democratic Party politicians as animals, such as United States Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Zohran Mamdani, the mayor of New York City, and former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton.
Former United States President Joe Biden, like the Obamas, is portrayed as an ape eating a banana.
According to the BBC, the video is believed to have originated from conservative meme creator Xerias, who shared the post on X in October 2025.

items.title: Göbeklitepe, Taş Tepeler and life 12,000 years ago exhibition opens in Berlin, Germany

s: On February 6, 2026, the "Gebaute Gemeinschaft - Göbeklitepe, Taş Tepeler and Life 12,000 Years Ago" exhibition opened at Berlin's James-Simon-Galerie.
Scheduled to be running until July 19, 2026, the show featured 93 archaeological artifacts brought from Turkey from Göbeklitepe and the Taş Tepeler region.
Stone sculptures from the UNESCO World Heritage site Göbeklitepe were exhibited alongside finds from Karahantepe, Sayburç, and Çakmaktepe.
Everyday objects and jewelry were on display.

Spanish photographer Isabel Muñoz's contemporary interpretations framing the hunter-gatherers' transition to settled life across eight thematic sections, which were exhibited in Spain earlier in 2024, were also included in the exhibition.
The exhibition was curated by Barbara Helwing (Vorderasiatisches Museum) and Necmi Karul (Istanbul University) in collaboration with Şanlıurfa Archaeology Museum and the Taş Tepeler research project.
It was the first time some exhibits were brought abroad, after having been exhibited in several locations in Turkey.

items.title: Caloundra through to next round of 2026 Australia Cup preliminaries

s: Caloundra have qualified for the next round of soccer's Australia Cup qualifiers with a 4-1 win over Pacific Pines on Saturday night in Meridan Plains, Queensland.
"[We had a] good second half," said Caloundra captain Kaine Frew.
"Obviously first competitive match [of the year] tonight.
It was good for the boys to get the cobwebs out.
We've played a few easier sort of preseason games and obviously they've come up from the Gold Coast."
Three goals in the space of ten minutes secured Caloundra's advancement after the scores were tied at 1 all at half time.
"We started a bit slow and obviously we got a few new players," Frew said.
"So we're all just still gelling.
But yeah, no, it was a really good second half.
We're happy with that.
And we'll take that into training next week and be ready for round one."
Caloundra's next game is scheduled to be against Brisbane Knights as part of the Football Queensland Premier League 2 opening round on February 28.
"[Brisbane Kights are] a big club, but we really don't know [what to expect], to be honest," said Frew.
"We're just going to worry about ourselves.
Obviously, we think we can be competitive this year there's no doubt about that.
As long as we can play 90 minutes.
Not like tonight where, you know, first half an hour wasn't great.
We need to play like we did in the second half for the whole game."

items.title: Musical performance presented by Striped Light in Long Island City, New York showcases four performers

s: On the evening of February 16, 2026, an audience gathered at an undisclosed location to see a performance by three experimental musical acts in Long Island City, Queens, New York, as part of the ongoing Striped Light series of events.
A volunteer contributor to Wikinews attended the event as a reporter.
There were somewhere between forty and a hundred people in attendance.
The doors opened for the event at 7:30 p.m.
New York time (0030 UTC).
Jennifer Gersten played the first set, as a soloist.
She played the violin using a variety of techniques, holding it in a traditional manner as well as on her lap at times.
Jack Langdon played the second set, also as a soloist.
He played a Native American flute through amplification, taking advantage of the opportunity to explore extended techniques and unusual sounds with the flute.
John King and Leyya Mona Tawil performed the third set as a duo.

King played guitar while using electronics and a laptop positioned on a table in front of him, while Tawil worked with electronics, multiple microphones, and unconventional objects; at one point, she danced on the amplified stage.
In contrast to the earlier sets, this was a high-volume set.
Striped Light is an ongoing series curated by David Watson and Ian Douglas-Moore.
The location of the performances is only revealed to performers and people who purchase tickets.

items.title: Green Party wins major by-election in northern England city of Manchester

s: The Green Party of England and Wales candidate Hannah Spencer has been declared the winner of Thursday's by-election in Gorton and Denton, a parliamentary constituency in Manchester, which was triggered following the resignation of the previous Labour MP Andrew Gwynne.
The election marks the first parliamentary by-election won by a Green Party candidate, and the first Green Party election win in the North of England.
Spencer will become the fifth current Green Party MP, with just under 41% of the vote, a lead of 12% on the second-place candidate, Matt Goodwin of Reform UK, who received just under 29% of the vote.
The election was highly anticipated as a test of confidence for the current Labour government, which has seen numerous high-profile scandals over past months.
The Labour candidate received 25% of the vote, dropping 25% from the 50% won at the 2024 general election.
The seat was previously regarded as the sixth safest seat for the party in Britain, and had not been lost by a Labour Party candidate since 1931.

Mayor of Greater Manchester Andy Burnham had applied to stand as the party's candidate, but was blocked by its National Executive Committee over a worry that Labour would lose the resulting by-election for Mayor, and amid fears he would mount a leadership challenge against Prime Minister Keir Starmer.

Former Deputy Leader of the Labour Party and former Deputy Prime Minister Angela Rayner said that "This result must be a wake up call" amid the election adding to mounting internal party pressure on Keir Starmer to resign following the election, which would trigger a leadership election within his party.
Starmer said in a statement that he was not planning to resign over the election results.
The Reform UK candidate Matt Goodwin's 29% of the vote was up 15% from the party's position in the constituency at the 2024 general election.

Talking to BBC News reporters, Goodwin blamed the Green Party win on "a coalition of Islamists and woke progressives that came together to dominate a constituency", and said "many people in this country will look at Gorton and Denton and be appalled by what they see."
The Conservative and Liberal Democrat parties both won just under 2% of the vote, with the Conservatives dropping 6% from the previous election, and the Liberal Democrats dropping 2%.

It is just the second time the Conservative Party has lost their deposit (which occurs by receiving under 5% of the vote) since 1962, and is the worst result in a by-election for the party in history.
The election and its campaign period has seen numerous allegations of misconduct.

The Reform campaign was alleged to have breached campaign laws by not imprinting statutory material clarifying the publisher on a public letter addressed from pensioner and Reform UK worker Patricia Clegg mailed to households in the constituency and printed to appear handwritten.
The Reform candidate Goodwin was acquitted by the High Court in a related case the day before the election.

The Green Party reported the Labour candidate Angeliki Stogia to police on election day after a campaign van not bearing the aforementioned imprint was pictured driving past polling stations, with text alleging the Greens wanted to "legalise all drugs and teach our children to use drugs" and "let our daughters be used for legal prostitution".
The Electoral Commission says on its website that campaigners must not drive or park vehicles "heavily branded with campaign material" near polling stations.

items.title: Caloundra wins first game in Australian soccer's Football Queensland Premier League 2 competition

s: Caloundra got their first season in the Football Queensland Premier League 2 (FQPL 2) competition underway with a 4 goals to 2 win over Brisbane Knights FC at their home ground in Meridan Plains, Australia on Saturday night.
"Starting the game that quickly, it just makes life a lot easier," Caloundra player Ethan Galbraith said.
"It was surprising but amazing at the same time.
I think we started fast like we wanted to.
And we got on top.
And once you do that to a team, obviously it makes it hard for them to get back into it.
But credit to them.
Second half with the man down, they really battled and made it difficult for us.
It's obviously a tough place to come.
Travel up the Coast on a weekend."
It was a tough away trip for the Brisbane Knights.
Their first twenty minutes were slow with a bit of ill-discipline, according to their coach, Rob Shaw.
"[It] cost us, I think, in that first half," Shaw said.
"[We] changed shape in the second half, showed, the boys settled, started to play football, a little bit better football.
It actually worked in some ways, even the man down.
The boys worked hard.
It was a bit of a mountain to climb, though, after the first half, but can't fault the effort though from the boys."
Caloundra will now travel to play Moreton City Excelsior while Brisbane Knights host the Samford Rangers.
"I think they're a pretty tough team," Galbraith said.
"We'll be up against it next week but looking forward to the challenge.
They've got a lot of good players in there. [They're a] very good team.
So we'll be up against it but ready for it."

items.title: Randwick City Council opens public consultation about parking near beaches: ''To pay or not to pay?''

s: On Wednesday, Randwick City Council, a municipality on the east coast of Sydney, New South Wales, Australia, opened a public consultation period focused on introducing parking fees at beaches within the Randwick area.
The consultation, affecting up to thousands of beachgoers in peak hours on hot summer weekends, is set to close on April 15.

The council mailed the consultation paper version to all residents and added to Randwick's "Have Your Say" portal with an online form and a note that feedback may also be provided by phone and in person.

The Council noted the beaches received a lot of non-local traffic, allegedly reaching 84% at certain beaches, according to mobile phone data collected by Veitch Lister Consulting (VLC), a United Kingdom and Australian firm.
The revenue from paid parking would help towards beaches cleaning, maintenance, and improving the quality of amenities, the Council wrote on the public consultation page.
The Council estimated implementing the proposal would require A$3.6 million expenditure and would generate yearly A$6 million revenue.
Randwick includes the Clovelly, Coogee, Maroubra, Malabar, Little Bay (Malabar Beach), La Perouse (Frenchmans Bay) and Yarra Bay areas.
The proposal stated that new signage and parking meters would be installed in late 2026 and 2027 if the proposal was approved.
A Wikinews contributor visited the area, noting previously the parking was time-limited but predominantly free, with selected sections designated as paid parking.
Parking at Arden St. was free, while parking at Coogee Oval or near Coogee Pavilion required a fee from 2003 to 2016.
Meanwhile, parking near Manly and Bondi beaches outside the Randwick area required a fee in many spots and streets immediately adjacent to the beach as of 2026.
Near Manly, a multi-level paid car park was available in a nearby shopping center.

items.title: US President Donald Trump appears to wear makeup after apparent rash breaks out on neck, reports say

s: On Tuesday, a rash that reporters had observed on US President Donald Trump's neck in photos from a Medal of Honor ceremony at the White House one day earlier appeared to have been covered up.
One media source indicated the substance used was cosmetic makeup, although Trump's physician, Dr. Sean Barbabella, told the source the rash had been covered up by a "very common cream."
President Trump has worn makeup in public before.
He once wore makeup to obscure bruises on his hands, which White House press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, stated were inflicted from "shaking hands all day every day.
Trump himself has attributed the bruises to his use of aspirin, of which he says he takes excessive amounts.
Trump said, "They say aspirin is good for thinning out the blood, and I don’t want thick blood pouring through my heart.
I want nice, thin blood pouring through my heart.
Does that make sense?"

items.title: Monta publishes its 2025 EV charger ranking, including hardware performance

s: The Danish firm Monta published a performance ranking of electric vehicle (EV) chargers on Wednesday.
The firm analysed 260,000 EV chargers connected to its platform, which were located in Europe.
In the publication, the firm showed the chargers ranked by their "performance score".
The firm calculated this score metric from two parameters — the charger uptime, and the percent of charge sessions that went successful without hardware or software or user interruptions.
The AC — slower chargers — and DC — fast chargers — ranking was provided in two separate tables.
AC chargers performance was topped by a Mennekes EV charger, with performance score 94.65.
Among DC chargers, five charger models by Alpitronic took the top spots, with performance score reaching 96.54.

The Driven, an Australian news site, noted that '9 out of 10' of the top performing DC chargers from Monta's report were available for sale, and were in use — by Ampol AmpCharge and BP Pulse — in Australia.
The firm noted the published results provided motivation for EV chargers to adopt these benchmarks in marketing, and further develop their products to increase performance and uptime.

A volunteer Wikinews reporter reached out to Monta, and Monta has clarified that they also have some EV chargers on their platform in Asia, Oceania, and North America, however excluded them from the ranking due to small quantities.
Monta also noted they were planning to release quarterly EV charger updates in 2026, and yearly EV charger ranking reports with awards.
The Monta's EV charger ranking program was launched in June last year.
Monta won the best EV app/software at the E-Mobility Awards 2023.

items.title: Moreton Bay illegally evicted homeless campers, Queensland Supreme Court rules
